en: The Buddha-dharma is boundless; humans and devas take refuge and pay homage. The five aggregates are all empty; the six sense faculties are purified. The wondrous scriptures abide forever;
if one reverently upholds them, the response is certain. The sea of suffering is difficult to cross.

The deities will support you so that you may attain self-composure; have no fear of calamitous kalpas. Simply maintain your original nature and recite [the mantra] with your mouth without ceasing. It will expel evil and dispel illness, and all phenomena will be realized as fleeting as lightning.

With a single mind like a mirror, you will finally awaken to your past causes. Suddenly and profoundly enlightened, you shall widely exhort the people of the world that this true word (mantra) is worthy of being heard.
Recorded with reverence by the Buddhist disciple Huang Lèzhī in the eighth month of autumn in the year of Wǔwǔ, the eighth year of the Xiánfēng era,
concerning the lineage of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.

The rise of the Śākya teaching began in the middle antiquity. Of old, there was a Sage named Dīpaṃkara, who turned the Great Wheel of Dharma to teach, transform, and deliver beings, whereby the Buddha-dharma first became manifest.

Reaching the year Jia-yin of King Zhao of Zhou, on the eighth day of the fourth month, Prince Siddhārtha—that is, Śākyamuni—was born to King Śuddhodana of Kapilavastu in India. [He possessed] the thirty-two...

[He possessed] the [thirty-two] marks and the eighty secondary characteristics. Due to his long-standing vows, he abandoned his kingdom to cultivate the Way. For six years at the Snowy Mountains, he engaged in profound contemplation and ascetic practices.

On the eighth day of the twelfth month, upon seeing the morning star appear, he attained sudden and complete enlightenment. Endowed with the six supernormal powers and supreme knowledge, he became the Honored One of the Three Realms.
He propagated the teachings in the Western Land, and thus the Buddha-dharma flourished greatly. After the Buddha first visited the Deer Park, later...
He resided at the Jeta Grove, where he expounded the Great Dharma for forty-nine years. At that time, there were several thousand people in the assembly listening to the Dharma together.
Among them was the great disciple, the Venerable Kāśyapa, who attained the Buddha’s treasury of the True Dharma;

the Buddha personally bestowed upon him a prediction of enlightenment, making him the first patriarch in the Western Land. There was also the Venerable Subhūti, whose life is wisdom, who was foremost in the realization of emptiness. There was...
The Venerable Śāriputra was foremost in wisdom; he was able to transmit the essential teachings of the Buddha’s mind.

The Second Patriarch, the Venerable Ānanda, was foremost in extensive learning; after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, he proclaimed the scriptural teachings, including the entire Prajñāpāramitā in six hundred fascicles.
All of these were what he transmitted. Later, during the reign of Emperor Ming of the Later Han, moved by a dream of a golden man, he dispatched envoys to India to seek out the Buddha-dharma.
The scriptures were carried back on white horses; it was from this point that the presence of the sacred texts in the Central Land began.

This lineage was transmitted to the twenty-eighth patriarch, the Venerable Bodhidharma, who, through his great supernormal powers, subdued the demonic heterodoxies of thirty-six locations and established a vast...
As for his vows: departing from Western India, he traveled across lands as numerous as the sands of the Ganges until reaching China, taking three full cycles of winter and summer.
He arrived at the South Sea on the twenty-first day of the ninth month of the seventh year of the Putong era of the Liang dynasty, the *gengzi* year.

There, he expounded the Dharma and disseminated the teachings, greatly opening the way for the Chan school. As for the transmission of its secret instructions, they generally derive from transcendent awakening, through which one clarifies the mind and realizes its true nature (*cittaprakṛti*).
He realized his original nature and became the First Patriarch in this Eastern Land.

Since the arrival of Bodhidharma from the West, he transmitted the seal of the mind to the Second Patriarch, Great Master Huik’e, and entrusted him with four fascicles of the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*, saying, "This is the essential gateway to the Tathāgata’s mind-ground;
let all sentient beings open, show, awaken to, and enter it. It was not until the time of the Fifth Patriarch, Great Master Hongren, that [the transmission] was first changed to...

Regarding the transmission of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, he once exhorted both monastics and laypeople that by simply upholding this sūtra, one would personally realize one's nature and attain Buddhahood.

Thus, when the Sixth Patriarch of Caoxi heard the passage from the sūtra, "One should give rise to the mind without dwelling on anything," he subsequently received the robe and bowl of the Fifth Patriarch.
It is therefore certain that the *Vajracchedikā* can bring about Buddhahood. This sūtra is the foremost [teaching] of the World-Honored One...
The Buddha preached this profound sutra across nine assemblies.

It was intended to resolve the various fevers of affliction for all sentient beings, transforming them into a realm of cool clarity, uprooting all suffering and distress, leading them out of the perils of the burning house, delivering all dark spirits, and enabling them to transcend the realms of hell.

It transforms those in the six realms of existence so they may attain the bliss of devas and humans; it is truly the lamp of wisdom for the dark alleys of ignorance and the compassionate vessel across the sea of suffering.

If a student of Chan can indeed sweep away all [phenomena], darkening the mind to inward contemplation, sitting in silent stillness and returning solely to emptiness—wherein emptiness itself has nothing to be emptied—and thus penetrating with unobstructed clarity, this constitutes the study of the unsurpassed Mahāyāna. This may be practiced whether morning or evening.

To recite and chant this with a faithful heart and uphold it, one may thereby understand the causes of past lives, escape the sufferings of the three miserable realms, extinguish sinful karma, and attain boundless merit.

Alas! In the midst of the turmoil and haste of life, from the crowing of the morning cock to the tolling of the evening bell, one may realize the wisdom of enlightenment and cross the ford of delusion by means of the precious raft.
Such is the Great Meaning of the West’s arrival; so it is, so it is. [End of] respective writings.
The efficacy of reciting the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* is as swift as the response of a shadow to a form or an echo to a sound; thus, I shall not elaborate further.

This scripture was designated by Prince Zhaoming of the Liang Dynasty as consisting of thirty-two sections (*fen*). However, upon carefully examining the paragraph divisions, I fear that...

Not only that; even each individual heading does not fully encompass the subject matter. For instance, the investigation into the four fruits of the śrāvaka path leading gradually to the state of a Tathāgata is directly connected to the section concerning the time at the place of Dīpaṃkara Buddha;
why then is it severed and attributed to the subsequent section on "Adornment"?

Furthermore, while the passage where the Venerable Subhūti asks about the faith of those who hear and accept the teaching follows upon the preceding text, it ultimately possesses its own distinct significance.
As for the requested [arrangement], one must not combine everything into a single part; rather, what remains should be divided or unified as appropriate, not merely following a single pattern.
This compilation of sections has synthesized the various traditions and adopted the most appropriate conclusions; it is not the result of mere arbitrary speculation.
Nevertheless, the thirty-two divisions have been handed down for a long time and must not be discarded. Herein, the titles designated for each division are listed.
Regarding the "End of the Eyebrows":
this sutra should be viewed as divided into sections. It is highly appropriate that Hanshan distinguished it into two volumes, upper and lower.

However, from the passage beginning with "The Great Assembly Arose" up to "One Immediately Sees the Tathāgata," it constitutes the entire main body of the Mahāyāna orthodoxy; specifically, it concerns abiding securely and subduing [the mind].
Without clinging to forms or appearances, the general purport of the entire sutra is hereby concluded. Thereafter, when Subhūti asks about true faith, [the Buddha] shows him purity;
when he asks about the name of the sutra, he shows him Prajñā; and when he asks about faith, understanding, and upholding, he shows him the arousal of the mind free from signs.
These points are revealed layer by layer, with an intention that is profound and deep. Furthermore, he subsequently praises this sutra...
"Excellent. [The Buddha] exhorted others to receive, uphold, read, and recite [this teaching], continuing until the section on the "Inconceivable.

All of these discuss the Dharma of Prajñāpāramitā, through which the meanings of abiding and subduing are cleansed and brought forth; this constitutes the first fascicle. Having heard what the Buddha had spoken, Subhūti...

Having deeply understood the meaning and intent, he even shed tears and wept with grief; how could he remain ignorant of the principle of abiding in submissiveness? He requested [the teaching] once more.

Later commentators have claimed that the former statement refers to coarse grasping while the latter refers to subtle grasping, and that the former was spoken for those who have newly resolved their minds, whereas the latter was spoken for those who have already resolved their minds. Both of these views are incorrect. This is because Subhūti feared...
For those virtuous men and women in future generations who have not yet personally received the Buddha’s words but have resolved their minds on Bodhi, there would be nothing to follow and practice.
The Buddha therefore wished to establish a single teaching to universally show to those who would come.

Thus, he refuted it by stating that "in reality, there is no dharma," subsequently explaining point by point the meanings left unfinished in the preceding fascicle; each contains a profound and subtle purport.
They do not correspond. At the end, it is revealed that one does not grasp at marks; suchness is immovable. This serves as the summary for the entire work.
The intent of "abiding" and "subduing" is thoroughly penetrated without omission; this constitutes the lower fascicle. The *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* lacks a first half.
If one expounds it without opening it up, there will be no second half; if one searches for and gathers it without exhausting it, this sutra must be viewed as a whole.
One fascicle is like a chapter; one chapter is like a phrase; one phrase is like a single character.
What is meant by a "single character"? Formerly, whenever Chan Master Zhaozhou encountered a student entering his room, he would have them investigate "Mu."
The character is taken as the *huatou*. This single character "Wu" (No) encompasses heaven and earth and contains all phenomena.
Having realized the principle of formlessness in the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, the entire scripture may be read as this one word.
This scripture provides an exegesis of its meaning, divided into three parts: commentary (*zhù*), treatise (*lùn*), and exposition (*jiǎng*). This format emulates the "Stone Commentary" edition.
"Commentary" (*zhù*) refers to breaking down each word and phrase of the primary text one by one. "Treatise" (*lùn*) refers to analyzing and judging the essential meanings of the original text.
"Exposition" (*jiǎng*) refers to unfolding and elucidating the meaning in accordance with the oral style of the Tathāgata and Subhūti. This applies to each section of the outline...
Regarding the organization of the textual structure and the transition between sections, I have supplemented the work with several passages from various commentaries.

These are analyzed in detail and divided into clear segments so that they do not become merely a mechanical stringing together of characters and phrases like teeth in a comb; rather, they allow for an interpretation of the meaning based on the text itself.
As for the sources selected, I initially relied on only four or five authors, but later obtained a compendium by Sun Shufu, which contains an exceptionally rich collection of materials.
There were originally several dozen families. Having further revised and edited them, they have been compiled into this single volume.

As for the names of the various families that are not fully recorded, it is because they are intermingled within the text and would be inconvenient to annotate individually; this is not intended to appropriate their merit.
In this sutra, the words of Ānanda’s compilation are marked with dots at the end of phrases; the words of Subhūti are marked with points; and the words of the Tathāgata are distinguished by circles.
Double circles are used for the essential key points throughout the entire text; linked circles are used for sections that are particularly refined, profound, and subtle;
and linked points are used for passages concerning efficacy. Furthermore, cross-references between preceding and succeeding sections are indicated as follows: [text continues]
Regarding the placement of the eyebrows and eyes, use a continuous line extending to the tips to make them distinct.
As for the essential method of reciting sutras,
why must it necessarily be done in a quiet room?
When people of the world recite the sutras, they mostly seek out quiet rooms; yet they fail to realize that steadfast sincerity resides entirely within the mind, not in the external environment.
If one’s fundamental mind is tranquil, even dwelling in a bustling marketplace is like being in a deep mountain forest. Observe those among our Confucian scholars who excel at reading:
some read while suspended from a tree branch, others carry their texts while weeding with a hoe, and they ultimately achieve success—not because of the study room.
How tranquil this is! Why must one necessarily leave the household life?

Leaving the household life was originally intended for the purpose of escaping all attachments and hindrances. Yet, I frequently see certain monks whose hearts of greed and attachment remain as they were before.
Such renunciation is, on the contrary, inferior to that of a layperson who practices the conduct of one who has left the home life; the latter becomes superior.
Observe the faithful laypeople of the past and present: those who attained awakening to Bodhi were exceedingly numerous, such as the Great Master Fu (Bodhidharma’s successor) and Layman Pang.
All of them possessed wives, children, and worldly entanglements, yet these did not obstruct their progress on the Path. One can thus know that [awakening] depends entirely upon nothing else.
One has left the household life.

Why must one set up images and face the Buddha to recite sutras? The intention is merely to arouse reverence in others; yet they do not realize whether such recitation is truly beneficial or not. It is simply...
In discussing whether the mind is sincere or not: if the mind is not sincere, even if one is never separated from the sacred image for a single moment, what benefit would there be?
Why then must one recite [the scriptures] with such haste?

Reciting the sutras consists entirely of reading the text aloud with the mouth while contemplating its meaning with the mind. It is essential that the words and phrases be clear and the subtle purport be thoroughly understood.

Even if one recites in a low, silent voice, it constitutes the supreme vehicle provided the intent is fully realized. However, if one rushes through the recitation, speaking indistinctly for the sake of speed, the words will reach the mouth but not the heart;
even if one has recited them ten thousand times, the meaning of the sutra will remain uncomprehended. This is fundamentally no different from...
Those who do not read [the scriptures] are the same as those who do; why must one kneel to recite and contemplate the meaning of the sutras?
Whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, there is no time that is unsuitable; why must one restrict oneself exclusively to kneeling?

Why must one provide a complete commentary on this entire sutra? Unless one examines it with meticulous detail, its wondrous meaning will not be clarified. If one is in a state of haste and busyness, how could one possibly read it in its entirety?
One must know that when worldly affairs are slightly at leisure, one should quiet the mind and read a single section; thus, one may grasp the meaning of that section.
As for its benefits: if one understands even a single section, one immediately gains the merit of that section.

Observe how, on that day, the Sixth Patriarch merely heard the line from the scripture, "One should give rise to the mind without dwelling anywhere," and immediately realized Bodhi. It is evident that this depends solely on the practitioner's mental awakening;
how could it be a matter of calculating the number of words and phrases?
According to the commentaries on the sutras, one may originally divide the text into sections at any time to study them in detail, aiming for understanding and realization;
it is indeed difficult to read the entire work at once. As for the recitation of the sutra text, this must be performed every day at the break of dawn.

Alternatively, after the fixed period of meditation has ended, when there are no longer disturbances from human affairs, one should settle the mind and sit upright, reciting with the mouth and contemplating with the mind.
Whether once or several times, one must strive to ensure that not a single thought arises. If one practices this for a long time, it will bring great benefit.

*Annotated Commentary on the Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, Fascicle One "Vajra" (diamond) refers to that which is among the hardest and sharpest of metals; "metal" (*kāñcana*) signifies the meaning of non-alteration, serving as a metaphor for the essence of *prajñā*.
This is what is called "reality-mark *prajñā*" (*bhūtalakṣaṇa-prajñā*). The mind is fundamentally without marks; it takes the true nature of the Tathāgata as its basis.
The true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) is precisely the innate purity of self-nature (*prakṛti-viśuddhi*). "Rigidly grasping" and "severing" signify its function, which is a metaphor for *prajñā*;

specifically, it refers to the *prajñā* of contemplative observation (*vipaśyanā-prajñā*). The mind is inherently endowed with awakening; when true wisdom manifests before one, this constitutes contemplative observation.
This is precisely the wondrous wisdom of original enlightenment (*prakṛti-āśraya-prajñā*). In Sanskrit it is *prajñā*; in Chinese it is "wisdom" (*zhìhuì*).
Wisdom (*jì*) is the essence of insight (*huì*), while insight is the function of wisdom. In Sanskrit it is *pāramitā*; in Chinese it is "reaching the other shore.

This shore refers to the realm where sentient beings perform karma and undergo suffering within the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*). The other shore refers to the ultimate transcendence of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
Liberation is the abode of purity and peace. One who possesses wisdom, remains free from all marks (*nimitta*), and maintains a constantly pure mind shall ascend to the other shore;
this is what is called Nirvāṇa. "Sūtra" means a path—it is the path for transcending the mundane and entering the state of sainthood.
In summary: *Vajra* is a metaphor; *Prajñā* is the Dharma; and *Pāramitā* is the realization of the fruit. This is it.
This was originally translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of the Yao Qin dynasty; it has been the most widely circulated. Regarding the treatise (*śāstra*):
this indicates the title of the sutra. There are six *pāramitās*: generosity overcomes stinginess and greed; ethical discipline overcomes lust and depravity;
patience overcomes anger and resentment; diligence overcomes indolence and retreat; meditative concentration overcomes distraction; and wisdom [overcomes ignorance].
Wisdom transcends ignorance; only Prajñā (transcendent wisdom) can give rise to the eighty-four thousand forms of wisdom.
Thus, the six perfections are fully encompassed and the myriad practices are all complete. Sentient beings harbor chaotic delusions and manifest a hundredfold deceptions;

they pride themselves on being clever, yet remain unaware that they are sinking into the ocean of suffering and will forever fall into the cycle of saṃsāra. These are truly ignorant people. The Buddha spoke thus.

The Sūtra states: May those who desire it, with a pure mind and wondrous wisdom, sever delusive conditions. With the luminosity of the nature of mind, may all ascend together to the shore of enlightenment.
For those who plant roots of goodness, they first recite the sūtras and ultimately awaken to the principle, attaining firm and unshakable power—this is the Vajra.
Possessing great wisdom—this is Prajñā. Crossing the ocean of birth and death to ascend the shore of Bodhi—this is the Wave.
This is the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā). The Great Master of the Fifth Patriarch once exhorted both monastics and laypeople:
"If you simply uphold the Diamond Sūtra, you will naturally be able to see your own nature and will certainly attain Buddhahood."
Thus have I heard. At one time the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, together with a great assembly of twelve hundred and fifty bhikṣus.
Then, at the time for eating, the World-Honored One put on his robes, took his bowl, and entered the great city of Śrāvastī to beg for food.
Having gone through the city begging for alms in due order, he returned to his original place and ate his meal.
[The discourse] concluded. Having gathered his robes and bowl and washed his feet, he spread out a seat and sat down.
*Annotation:* "Thus" (*iti*) refers to the entire sutra. "I" (*aham*) is Ānanda referring to himself;

it signifies that what is spoken in this sutra was personally heard by him from the Buddha. "At one time" (*ekasmin samaye*) refers to the time when the sutra was preached. "Buddha" refers to Śākyamuni.

"Muni" is a Sanskrit term; in the language of China, it means "Awakened. Because he has awakened himself and awakened others, and because his practice of awakening is perfected, he is called a Buddha.
Śrāvastī is the capital where King Prasenajit resided. Jeta was the king’s crown prince.
These trees were planted by Jeta’s own hand, hence they are called the Jetavana (Jeta’s Grove). As for the Anāthapiṇḍika Garden, [it was established by] the king’s minister, Anāthapiṇḍika...
Dhana was known as the Elder Anāthapiṇḍada because he provided relief to the poor. Susadana held the Buddha’s teachings in profound reverence;
he borrowed a garden from Jeta and together they constructed a vihāra, inviting the Buddha to preach the Dharma.

Therefore, the Buddha resided permanently in that garden with the bhikṣus—“bhikṣu” being the Chinese term for “one who begs. [The bhikṣu] begs the Dharma from the Buddhas above and begs food from the faithful below.
This means: "The great bhikṣus" refers to those who have attained the profound path. "Together" means being in the same place.

According to the account, when the Buddha attained enlightenment, he first ordained the five men, including Kauṇḍinya; next, he ordained the three Kāśyapa brothers along with their thousand followers;
next, he ordained Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana, each with one hundred disciples; and next, he ordained Yaśas... [text continues].
The sons of the elder Śreṇika and others, fifty in number, should thus total one thousand two hundred and fifty-five people;
the sutra here cites the larger figure for brevity. Because the Buddha is honored by all within the three realms, he is called the World-Honored One (Bhagavān). The various devas eat at dawn.
The various ghosts eat in the evening; the Buddhas eat at midday. "Mealtime" refers to the hour of noon.
As for the robe, it is the great robe of thirty-five strips, patterned like a water field with its boundaries demarcated. As for the bowl, it is a bowl of dark-blue lapis lazuli.
Because the Buddha walks barefoot, he washes it. "To spread" means to lay out; whenever the Buddha preaches the Dharma, he invariably spreads out a sitting mat.
Treatise: This introduction explains the causes and conditions for the Buddha’s teaching. The Buddha was a prince of the Golden Wheel;
who would not have made offerings to him? Yet he still practiced begging, desiring to undergo the ascetic practices of *dhūta* to show himself as equal to ordinary monks.
He did this so that the monastics of future generations would not accumulate assets, abandon their greedy minds, humble their arrogance, and thereby refine their spiritual nature (*gotra*).

Furthermore, the Buddha-dharma must consist of three essentials: namely, precepts (*śīla*), concentration (*samādhi*), and wisdom (*prajñā*). Begging for food is the precept; sitting cross-legged is concentration.
The precepts can support concentration, and concentration can give rise to wisdom. Therefore, one employs precepts and concentration to initiate the primary teaching of Prajñā.

The discourse was spoken by Ānanda: "I have heard that when the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the park of the householder Anāthapiṇḍada, with one thousand two hundred and fifty bhikṣus seated beneath him, it was then exactly midday, the time for taking food.
The Buddha then donned his saṃghāṭī robe and took up the alms bowl offered by the Four Heavenly Kings."
He entered the city of Śrāvastī from the outside and went on his alms round in successive order. He did not bypass the poor to seek the wealthy, nor did he abandon the lowly to follow the noble;
with equanimity and without distinction, he begged for food in a uniform manner. Having returned to the grove, he finished his meal.
About to enter meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), he thereupon gathered his robes and bowl, thereby setting aside all external requisites. He washed his feet, purifying his physical karma.
He spread out his seat, withdrawing movement to return to stillness; thus did the origin of the preaching of the Dharma begin.

At that time, the Elder Subhūti was among the great assembly. He rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms in reverence, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"It is rare, World-Honored One! The Tathāgata skillfully protects and sustains all bodhisattvas;
he skillfully entrusts all bodhisattvas. World-Honored One, those good men and good women who have resolved upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*..."
"Regarding the mind set on *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, how should it abide? How should one subdue that mind?
The Buddha said, "Excellent, excellent, Subhūti! Just as you have said, the Tathāgata well protects and sustains all bodhisattvas and well entrusts all bodhisattvas.
Listen attentively now; I shall speak for you. Son of good family, daughter of good family, having generated the mind for..."
"The mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* should be established in this way, and its mind should be subdued in this way.

'Yes indeed, World-Honored One; I wish to hear [your teaching]. (The phrase 'how should it be established' here differs from the later 'how should one establish oneself. This is because the former asks about the practical application of the practice, while the latter asks for the instruction on the Dharma.
The intent of the sutra is thus distinct.)"
Note: "At that time" refers to the moment when the meal was finished and he was seated at ease. "Elder" (*sthavira*) is a title for one of advanced age and great virtue.

Subhūti was foremost among those who understood emptiness (*śūnyatā*) and was ranked among the ten great disciples. Since the nature of absolute emptiness is truly *bodhi* (enlightenment), he is named Subhūti.
Because the nature of emptiness gives rise to all phenomena, he is also called Śūnyatā-ja (Born of Emptiness). The nature of emptiness follows...

He manifests in accordance with conditions to benefit people and things; he is thus also named "Good Manifestation" (Subhūti). The left represents the heterodox, while the right represents the orthodox, signifying the meaning of abandoning the heterodox to return to the orthodox.
Baring the shoulder signifies taking full responsibility for the burden. Kneeling on the ground signifies bending one's self in humble compliance.
With palms joined, the mind merges with the Way, and the Way merges with the mind. These are all the protocols for practicing reverence.

"Rare indeed!"—these are words of praise for the Buddha. "Tathāgata" is a general title for a Buddha. "Tathā" (Thus) refers to the essential substance of true nature; "Āgata" (Come) refers to the functional application of true nature.
This is the meaning of being tranquil and unmoving, yet responding and thereby penetrating all things. "Rakṣa" (Protect) means to guard against...
"Bias" refers to partiality and depravity. "To mind" means to guard with urgency. "To entrust" means to transmit by way of the Right Path. "To charge" means to hand over with earnestness.
"Bodhisattva" is a term from the Flower Language (Sanskrit) meaning "Awakened Being"; it refers to one who is able to awaken themselves and also to awaken sentient beings.
This term refers to those who study under the Tathāgata. The two phrases beginning with "The Tathāgata skillfully guards" introduce the entire sutra; hereafter, all...
All that the Buddha has spoken is a protective mindfulness and an entrustment.
