Pure faith is the root of goodness (*kuśalamūla*) by which sentient beings can become Buddhas and patriarchs.
These three lines are addressed to all sentient beings; they are spoken with earnest exhortation, seeking directly to awaken those who are still dreaming.
Lecture: Having heard the teaching on the True Principle of the Mahāyāna, Subhūti feared that future sentient beings might be unable to give rise to faith.
He thereupon addressed the Buddha, saying: "The World-Honored One has taught that there are no bodhisattvas who do not reverently uphold [this Dharma].
Yet, if ordinary people in the final age were to hear such words and phrases, would they truly be able to give rise to genuine faith? The Buddha—
He said: "Do not speak thus. This principle of signless, true emptiness can only be trusted by those with a profound foundation;
even if it were five hundred years after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa."
If there is a person who upholds the precepts, extensively cultivates fields of merit, and can have firm conviction that these words and phrases are true,
such a person must be one who has severed evil karma and planted roots of goodness at the source from which all Buddhas arise.
If such a person possessing these roots of goodness hears these words and phrases of this sutra, even for a single thought-moment—
Within this state, their minds are constantly pure; they believe with firm conviction and without doubt. This mind then merges with that of the Tathāgata.
The Buddha’s wisdom and insight know all their thoughts and behold all their actions.
These sentient beings shall thereby obtain immeasurable, pure merit and virtue. Why is this? It is because these sentient beings have realized the emptiness of true suchness.

Regarding the principle of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*): there are no longer the four characteristics of self, person, sentient being, or life-span; this is the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*).

Since these four characteristics are empty, all phenomena (*dharma*) have no basis upon which to be established. Therefore, one does not cling to existence as the characteristic of phenomena, nor does one cling to non-existence as the characteristic of non-phenomena;
this is the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*). Why is this so? Because these sentient beings, if their minds...
It is not empty or pure; one then becomes attached to the traces of self, person, multitude, and life-span. This is easy for such a person to understand.
As for my teaching that there is no mark of dharmas (*dharmalakṣaṇa*), it is because my true suchness (*tathatā*) as the fundamental substance does not reside within language or written characters.
If one grasps at the mark of dharmas, it is the same as being attached to the four marks (*catur-lakṣaṇa*). If one grasps at the mark of non-dharmas (*adharmalakṣaṇa*), furthermore...
This involves falling into the view of annihilationism; how does it differ from the previous attachment to the four marks?
Therefore, one should not grasp at the mark of dharmas and consider them as existent, nor should one grasp at the mark of non-dharmas and consider them as non-existent.
Thus, within the essence of nature, form and trace are entirely forgotten. This principle also has its source, for the Buddha once said:
"You who study the Way should know that when I preach this Dharma, it is because you are unable to realize true emptiness and transcend to the other shore.
I merely employ this Dharma as a provisional means to deliver you from the bitter sea of birth and death.
Once you have personally seen your own original nature and realized the bliss of Nirvana, then my Dharma will have no further use for you. It is, for example,"
One uses a raft to ferry people across; once they have reached the shore, the raft is no longer of use.

Viewed from this perspective, even that which is "Dharma" should be relinquished, let alone that which is "non-Dharma. Furthermore, how could one cling to non-existence, sinking into emptiness and guarding silence?
"Subhūti, what do you think? Has the Tathāgata attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*?

Or has the Tathāgata preached any dharma? Subhūti replied, "As I understand the meaning of what the Buddha has taught, there is no fixed dharma named *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, nor is there any fixed dharma that the Tathāgata can [attain or preach]."
Why is this? Because all dharmas taught by the Tathāgata are ungraspable and ineffable; they are neither dharmas nor non-dharmas.
Why is this? It is because all noble ones (ārya) are distinguished precisely by means of the unconditioned dharma (asaṃskṛta-dharma).
Commentary: "Obtaining" (de) means to obtain for oneself. "Explaining" (shuo) means to teach others. Regarding the character "yi" (meaning/significance), it appears here because of this significance;
it specifically refers to the teaching that one should not grasp at dharmas nor grasp at non-dharmas. There is no fixed [position].

It is neither exclusively existent nor exclusively non-existent; it speaks of both the Dharma and the non-Dharma. However, at that time, Subhūti had not yet fully realized that all dharmas are "not-all-dharmas.

Therefore, he did not say directly that there are no dharmas, but rather that there is no fixed dharma that can be grasped—meaning it cannot be grasped by means of the marks of form—and that it cannot be spoken of—meaning it cannot be expressed.
To speak with the mouth and tongue: that which is "not the Dharma" exists yet is absent; that which is "not non-Dharma" is absent yet is present.

O worthy one, as for the four fruits [of the path] and their like, they are the sages—the Buddhas. To explain them by means of characters is to provide an interpretation through the function of words.
Unconditioned dharmas are the nature of pure awakening; they do not depend on human effort.
They are non-abiding, they are signless, and they are unsurpassed bodhi. Elder, you first spoke of non-fixation, and subsequently spoke of the unconditioned.
This is the entry into the sacred realm.
Treatise: This follows upon the preceding [point] that one must not grasp at dharmas nor grasp at non-dharmas, thereby clarifying the true Dharma which is neither attained nor expounded.
The previous text stated: "If one sees all marks as non-marks, then one sees the Tathāgata. These two...

This sentence encompasses the essential purport of the entire sutra. However, when one encounters the term "Tathāgata," if it falls upon the level of *dharmatā* (the true nature of reality), it becomes a mark of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*);
if it falls upon the level of non-appearance (*animitta*), it becomes a mark of non-phenomena (*adharmalakṣaṇa*).

Therefore, while the preceding section cleared away both paths of "dharma" and "non-dharma," this section instead interrogates the Tathāgata regarding what he has attained and what he has taught. These two...

The character for "Tathāgata. When looking at the root of the upright [mind], one sees the character for "Tathāgata" appearing. One must examine where his point of faith falls; it is settled right there.
Śāriputra answered that there is no fixed dharma and that it cannot be grasped or explained. It is lively and active, precisely within this very state.
At the end, he spoke of the distinction between unconditioned dharmas; this is not merely a matter of standing on solid ground.
How could the Grounds (bhūmi) be described so accurately? This single phrase is spoken for the sake of sentient beings;
it enables them to transcend birth and death and proceed toward Bodhi. Therefore, the subsequent passage proceeds to compare the merit of upholding this sutra.
Commentary: Having previously explained that dharmas have characteristics and that non-dharmas do not, the Buddha feared that Subhūti had not yet fully penetrated this.
Therefore, he asked: "Do you truly perceive within yourself the attainment of the dharma of the Tathāgata’s unsurpassed bodhi?"
"Is it by means of this Dharma that one speaks and instructs others?

Subhūti replied, "According to how I have realized the meaning of what the Buddha has taught in my own mind, I know that the Dharma of Unsurpassed Bodhi is originally, from the beginning, true emptiness;
it has never designated a single dharma as being named 'Unsurpassed Bodhi. This is precisely what the Buddha has taught."
The teachings are established randomly from week to week; how could they ever designate a single fixed method, requiring that one must practice in such-and-such a way?
Why is this so? The unsurpassed Dharma of Bodhi taught by the Tathāgata can be cultivated through one’s inherent nature, but cannot be grasped through external forms.
It can be transmitted through the mind, but cannot be conveyed through words. If one clings to it as being a substantial dharma...

The nature of my self is void and numinous, beyond measure; it is not a "dharma" (a fixed entity). Yet, if one clings to the notion that it is a "non-dharma," my nature nevertheless responds immediately to conditions;
thus, it is also not a "non-dharma. Indeed, the dharma of unsurpassed bodhi is entirely my own natural awakened nature, without reliance on artificial human effort.
Therefore, all worthies and sages are identical to this unconditioned dharma. Thus says the Sage.
Because they are fully endowed with purity, they are called "noble" (ārya). Because Bodhisattvas awaken through their own vocal teachings, they become "worthy" (bhadra).
Such is the distinction between what they realize.

"Subhūti, what do you think? If someone were to fill a trichiliocosm with the seven treasures and give them as a gift, would the merit obtained by that person be great? Subhūti replied, "It would be very great, World-Honored One."
Why is this? Because that merit is not the nature of merit; therefore, the Tathāgata says that the merit is great.

The Buddha said, "Subhūti, if there were another person who, from this sutra, were to receive, uphold, and even explain as little as a four-line verse for others, their merit would surpass the former. Why is this? Subhūti, all..."
The Buddhas and the dharmas of the *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* of all Buddhas—all emerge from this sutra.
Subhūti, that which is called "Buddha-dharma" is not Buddha-dharma; it is merely designated as "Buddha-dharma."
Note: "Three-thousandfold Great Thousandfold World" refers collectively to the great world-system. The "seven treasures" are gold, silver, lapis lazuli, coral, agate, pearl, and crystal.
This giving is viewed as an act of relinquishment. "Merit" (puṇya) refers to cultivating the virtue of giving and enjoying blessings in the present life.
"The nature of merit" (puṇyatā) refers to cultivating the virtue within the [ultimate] nature. Wisdom...

That which is illuminated by light possesses a share of merit that transcends ordinary men; this is precisely the True Nature (*tathatā*). The Venerable One attained realization and pointed out the single character "nature" (*xìng*).
This is most worthy of focused attention. Faith-power is called "receiving," and mindfulness-power is called "upholding. When speech forms a sentence, it becomes a verse (*gāthā*).
A "four-line verse" may refer to two verses from a sutra, or it may refer to the four lines concerning the mark of non-self (*anātman*). —Guifeng.

That is to say: regarding all marks (*nimitta*), the four lines [of verse] are most sublime. One must know that this is derived from the practice of receiving and upholding (*udgrahaṇa*) as taught in the sutras;
there must be the word "up to" (*yāvat*) at the beginning and the word "etcetera" (*ādi*) at the end.

This means that within this sutra, one may receive and uphold a single section, a single chapter, or even as little as a four-line verse (*gāthā*). There is a range from many to few; the meaning is not restricted to a single verse alone. How could it be otherwise?
One grasps the four propositions in order to find a point of attachment within the Dharma of Bodhi—meaning that all Buddhas seek the Dharma of true nature.
What Buddha is not mind? What Buddha-Dharma is not a dharma of mind? This sutra is the true reality (*tattva*) of Prajñā;
therefore, it is said that "all [dharmas] emerge from this sutra. This does not refer merely to the words and phrases of the text. As for "Buddha-Dharma," it is the truth.
The principle of the Truths is not that which clings to dharmas by those who do not possess the Buddha-dharma; that which is called the Buddha-dharma is not annihilationism.
Treatise: This is the first instance of comparing merit. There are nine successive comparisons of merit.

Each meaning has its own specific application. This Buddha feared that people, because of the teaching that "nothing can be grasped," might dwell in a state of signlessness and unconditionedness, thereby wishing to discard the verbal instructions.
If the verbal instructions were discarded, by what means would one attain faith and understanding?
Therefore, he specifically pointed out that the Dharma of unsurpassed Bodhi all originates from the Prajñā of letters; for the human mind inherently possesses it.
Buddha-nature is realized only after relying upon the provisional Prajñā of words; therefore, this sutra is the true nature of Prajñā, capable of giving birth to the Buddha-dharma.
Yet, fearing that people might develop further attachments toward the Buddha-dharma itself, he immediately offers a turning phrase, saying:
"The Buddha-dharma is not the Buddha-dharma. This is because the Buddha-dharma resides in the mind and not in the teachings; it is not the Buddha-dharma [in the sense of being a fixed entity].
This means there is no mark of dharmas. That which is called "Buddha-dharma" likewise has no mark of non-dharmas.
Throughout the sutras, whenever the phrase "that which is thus is not" appears—marking the point where the brush is bent three times—it always contains these two meanings.

Every time the Buddha preached a discourse, he invariably compared it with the merit gained through giving; for the Buddha knew that during the age of the Dharma’s decline, many [would fall into error].
One should practice with generosity and relinquishment. Because [people] do not understand the essential point of seeing the nature, I have spoken of it earnestly and repeatedly.
As for the previous discussion, I stated that phenomena are unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). The Buddha feared that people might overlook the words and phrases of the Prajñā[pāramitā]; therefore, he...
Regarding the comparison of the merit of upholding this sutra, a question was posed:
"If someone were to fill the trichiliocosm with the seven treasures and offer them as a gift, would the merit obtained by that person be great?
Subhūti replied, "It would be very great. However, he added, "That merit is a gift characterized by signs; it does not accord with my nature of true emptiness and non-existence."
The characteristics of the wondrous Dharma are entirely unrelated [to such merit]; it ultimately does not possess the nature of true merit.
Therefore, what the Tathāgata calls "merit" is merely the cause for the minor fruits of humans and devas; this is why it is said to be "much. The Buddha further said:
suppose there were another person who, within this sutra, believed and accepted its words and upheld its meaning, even down to a single four-line verse.
If one further explains this to others, then awakening oneself and awakening others, the merit thereof far exceeds that of giving the seven treasures.
For the latter is a giving performed while dwelling in signs; even if it yields turbid blessings, once those blessings are exhausted, one falls back into decline.
This, however, is to awaken one's nature through the sutra; its merit is equal to the great void and remains indestructible throughout kalpas. Is its merit not vastly superior?
Why is this so? It is because this sutra is the path of practice.
The bodies of all Buddhas and the dharmas they have realized are all born from the *prajñā* of letters; beyond this, there is no other sutra.
Now, the dharma of unsurpassed bodhi is precisely the Buddha-dharma. However, that which is called the Buddha-dharma is fundamentally non-existent.
There is. It does not go beyond causing one to see one's nature beneath words; this is what is merely called "Buddha-dharma" by a provisional name.
*Huìjiě* (Comprehensive Explanation): From Subhūti’s question regarding true faith up to this point, there are three sections forming one unit.
There is no person and no dharma; sentient beings practice without marks (*animitta*). There is no attainment and no teaching; the Tathāgata’s preaching of the Dharma is without [marks].
This is the characteristic mark. When Subhūti spoke the two words "unconditioned" (*asaṃskṛta*), the true essence of Prajñāpāramitā was already made clear.
The Buddha feared that people might mistake the unconditioned dharma for a state of withered stillness and remain stuck therein;

they fail to realize that as soon as Bodhi manifests, all dharmas are fully present, and the merit of the true nature is immeasurable and boundless. It is precisely for this reason [that he spoke thus].
The Sūtras are the very nature of Prajñā, the path to attaining Buddhahood; nothing lies outside of this. Buddhists awaken to this nature through the Sūtras;
it is not merely a matter of recitation and exposition.
"Subhūti, what do you think? Does a stream-enterer have this thought: 'I have attained the fruit of stream-entry'?
Subhūti replied, "No, World-Honored One. Why is that? A stream-enterer is called one who has entered the stream, yet there is nothing entered;
they do not enter form, sound, smell, taste, touch, or dharmas. This is called a stream-enterer. Subhūti, at that time...
“What do you think, Subhūti? Does a once-returner (sakṛdāgāmin) have this thought: ‘I have attained the fruit of a once-returner’?
Subhūti replied, “No, World-Honored One. Why is that? A ‘once-returner’ is so called because they return once more; yet in reality, there is no coming or going.”
This is called a Sakṛdāgāmin. Subhūti, what do you think? Does an Anāgāmin have this thought: ‘I have attained the fruit of an Anāgāmin’?
Subhūti replied: “No, World-Honored One. Why is that? An Anāgāmin is so named because he does not come back;
yet in reality there is no such thing as ‘not coming back. For this reason, he is called an Anāgāmin. Subhūti, what do you think?
"How is it? Can an Arhat have this thought: 'I have attained the path of Arhatship'?
Subhūti replied, "No, World-Honored One. Why is this? Because, in reality, there is no dharma named 'Arhat.
World-Honored One, if an Arhat were to have this thought, 'I have attained the path of Arhatship,' he would then be clinging to a self, a person, a sentient being, or a life-span."
"World-Honored One, the Buddha has declared that I have attained the samādhi of non-contention and am foremost among men;
I am a *arhat* who is foremost in being free from desire. World-Honored One, I do not harbor the thought, 'I am an *arhat* free from desire.
World-Honored One, if I were to harbor the thought, 'I have attained the path of an *arhat*,' then the World-Honored One would not say that Subhūti delights in [emptiness]."
“Āraṇa-vihārin,” Subhūti, because you actually have no practice at all, you are named ‘Subhūti who delights in the practice of araṇā.
The Buddha said to Subhūti: ‘What do you think? When the Tathāgata was formerly with Dīpaṃkara Buddha, was there any dharma [attained]?’”
"Was there anything obtained? No, World-Honored One. When the Tathāgata was with the Buddha Dīpaṃkara, he truly obtained nothing regarding the Dharma.
(In the present text, this is called 'Anāgāmin'; the character for 'non-existence' is absent)."
Note: "One who can form this thought" refers to one who has previously conceived the aspiration to attain the Way.

The four preceding instances of the word "I" are terms used to represent the conceptualizations of those who have attained the four fruits [of the śrāvaka path]. In the Buddha-dharma, there is both cause and fruit; one must be able to cultivate the cause.
One immediately attains this fruit: Srotāpanna. In the language of China, this means "entering the stream," which refers to entering the stream of the sages.
"Having nothing to enter" means not being attached to the marks of entering the stream. This is the first fruit of the Śrāvaka. One who awakens through the teachings of sound is called a Śrāvaka.
Sakṛdāgāmin. In the language of China, this means "one who comes and goes once. This means coming once to the heavens and [returning once to the human realm].
Having come into the human realm, one may immediately attain nirvana. The Sixth Patriarch said: "If the preceding thought gives rise to delusion, the succeeding thought should immediately cease it.
If the preceding thought has attachment, the succeeding thought should immediately detach from it. Even when the eyes behold various objects, this mind still undergoes arising and ceasing."
There is no second birth or death; therefore, it is said that there is "one coming and going. In reality, there is no one who comes and goes, for there is no characteristic of coming and going.
This is the second fruit of the śrāvaka, which ranks one level above the stream-enterer (srotāpanna).

Anāgāmin—translated into Chinese as "not returning"—means that one is born directly into the heavens of the four dhyānas and does not return to take birth in the desire realm. In reality, there is no...
"Coming" refers to not being attached to the mark of coming. This is the third fruit of the śrāvaka, which still involves "coming and going.
One level higher than this is the arhat; in the Chinese language, this means "non-arising.

It signifies that all outflows (*āsrava*) have been exhausted and there are no further afflictions, such that one will no longer undergo birth within the three realms. The arhat attains the principle of signlessness (*animitta*). People...
The dharmas are both empty; they have already realized nirvāṇa. This is yet one level higher than the path of the śrāvaka.
Since the path is already perfected to the utmost, it is not called a "fruit" but is termed a "path. "In truth, there is no dharma" means that there are no afflictions to be abandoned.

There is no greed or anger to be abandoned; the mind is free from both the favorable and the adverse. Subject and object are both forgotten, such that not even a hair’s breadth of a phenomenon can be grasped.
As for "non-contention": where there is desire, there is contention; since this state is free from desire, what contention could there be?

*Samādhi* is the Chinese term for "right view," referring to the mind of original enlightenment (*mūla-vidyā*). To be "free from desire" means to have completely severed the afflictions of views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa* and *bhāvanā-kleśa*).
*Arana* is the Chinese translation for "quiescence" (*śānti*). "Joy" (*le*) means "to like" or "to prefer," referring here to a preference for pure conduct.

This is because the Buddha once spoke these words, and Subhūti cites them as proof. "In truth, there is nothing practiced" means that the fundamental nature is empty and quiescent, and thus one does not cling to the characteristics of practice.
From the words "The Buddha said... onwards, the Venerable One describes his own realization.

This is to realize the signless (*animitta*). The above has discussed the four fruits [of the śramaṇa], all of which consist of unconditioned dharmas (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*) and do not involve attachment to the signs of attaining those fruits.
Below, this is further corroborated by the signlessness of the Buddha. "Tathāgata" refers to Śākyamuni.
Dīpaṃkara Buddha is none other than Dīpaṅkara Buddha; he was the teacher of Śākyamuni.

"Truly there is nothing to be attained" means that the realization of Buddhahood arises from the awakening of one's own fundamental mind, and that there is no dharma whatsoever that can be attained. The character "real" (shí) here corresponds to the "numerical reality" (shí) mentioned above.

Treatise: This passage sequentially examines the points of cultivation and realization of all worthies and sages; in every case, they rely upon the unconditioned dharma (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*) and do not grasp at marks (*nimitta*).
Although the efforts toward the four fruits of arhatship possess their own respective grades, with each fruit realized, it is simultaneously realized as empty.
Regarding the first fruit, it is said that one "does not enter into form, sound, odor, taste, touch, or dharmas. Thus we know that sensory objects of desire must be avoided, just as...

The first fruit is called "the newly born. The second fruit is called "once-returner" (*sakṛdāgāmin*); this means that having entered the realm of desire once, one does not return, like a large fruit on its way to ripening.
The third fruit is called "non-returner" (*anāgāmin*); this means that having departed from the realm of desire, one leaves it as if it were cast away, like a fully ripened fruit.

The fourth fruit is called "detachment from desire" (*vītarāga*); this means being liberated such that there is not even a trace of desire to be removed, like a fruit already harvested. Such is the gradual teaching.
If one suddenly awakens to the true emptiness of unsurpassed bodhi, then by means of this very Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā, one transcends directly into the stage of Buddhahood.
What need is there then to speak of the four fruits of the śrāvaka path? The Buddha himself said that in attaining Buddhahood, there is truly nothing to be attained;
he realized the non-attainment of the four fruits. To speak of the principle of formlessness is simply to realize what belongs to oneself inherently.
True nature: that one attains Buddhahood is entirely through the self-awakening of one's own mind. Regarding all phenomena, there is nothing to be attained;
they fundamentally belong to the reality-mark (*dharmatā*), and are not subject to annihilation.
The discourse: Subhūti spoke of unconditioned dharmas (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*) and had already realized the practice of a bodhisattva.
The Buddha then questioned him by distinguishing [him] from the unconditioned state of the noble ones (*ārya*), saying: "Does a stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*) ever think:
'Will I certainly attain this fruit'? Subhūti replied: "No. A stream-enterer has entered among the noble ones."
"Stream-enterer" (Srotāpanna) means one who has entered the stream; yet, the mind has nothing to attain and does not cling to the marks of entering the stream.
It is simply that one has not yet suddenly realized true emptiness (*śūnyatā*), but is merely able to refrain from entering the realms of the six sense-objects.
This is why one is called a Srotāpanna—is it not so? The Buddha said: "A Sakṛdāgāmin once had this thought: 'Will I certainly attain this fruit? Subhūti..."
Subhūti replied, "No, World-Honored One. A Sakṛdāgāmin goes once to the heavens and returns once to the human realm; thus he is called 'One Who Comes Once.
Yet his mind attains nothing, for he does not cling to the marks of coming and going.

This is because he has already realized the ultimate emptiness of true reality and is able to transcend birth and death, no longer subject to the cycle of saṃsāra. Is it for this reason that he is named a Sakṛdāgāmin? The Buddha said:
Anāgāmin once had this thought: "Will I certainly attain this fruit? Subhūti said: "No.
An Anāgāmin does not come back to be born in this world; thus he is called 'Non-returner. Yet, in his mind there is nothing attained, and he does not cling to the mark of non-returning.
This is because his fundamental nature is luminous, empty, and without self; within, he has no desire-mind, and without—"
It is a realm free from desire; it is named *anāgāmin*. Is it for this reason? The Buddha asked, "Does an *arhat* ever have such a thought as:
'Will I surely attain this path'? Subhūti replied, "No. An *arhat* has purified all conditions;
externally they are like wood or stone—unmoving and unshakable. Their mind is like still water, neither seeping nor leaking; their nature is [thus]."
In this fundamental true emptiness, there is not a single dharma that can be apprehended; it is for this reason that one is called an Arhat.

Is it not so, World-Honored One? If an Arhat were to harbor the thought that they have attained the Way, they would immediately become attached to the four marks of self, person, multitude, and life-span.

"Therefore, the Buddha once said that because I do not give rise to a single thought and do not conflict with others, I have attained the Samādhi of Non-contention (*araṇā-samādhi*) and am foremost among his disciples.
It must be that I have completely shed human desires and severed these thoughts that the Buddha regards me as an Arhat free from desire.
If I were to harbor such a thought, I would not be able to attain Arhatship."
When the Way of the Han arose, he further gave rise to deluded thoughts, thinking: "The Buddha did not say that I am a person who delights in tranquility.

Subhūti, although there are outward manifestations of my practice, there is not a single thing to be grasped within my mind; therefore, the Buddha names me one who delights in the practice of *araṇā*.
The Buddha ultimately feared that the mind which had attained this state was not yet eliminated, and so he continued to transform him through silent influence.
[The Buddha] said: "When I was originally with Dīpaṃkara Buddha, did I truly obtain the Dharma of my original teacher? Subhūti replied:
"No. Although the Tathāgata’s single mind was pure while he was with Dīpaṃkara Buddha, it was merely due to the teacher’s guidance;
in reality, he attained awakening and cultivation through himself, and regarding the Dharma, there was truly nothing to be obtained."
"Subhūti, what do you think? Does a bodhisattva adorn buddha-fields? "No, World-Honored One. Why is that?
That which is called 'adorning a buddha-field' is not actually adorning; it is merely named 'adornment.
Therefore, Subhūti, all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should give rise to a pure mind in this way: they should not give rise to a mind dwelling upon form."
When the mind arises in response to sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or dharmas, one should give rise to that mind without dwelling on anything.
(Commentary: Adornment refers to such acts as building stupas and monasteries, or creating images for offering, throughout a single great world-system.

There must be a Buddha who establishes a transformation; this is called a buddha-field (*buddhakṣetra*). With golden ground and forests of the seven treasures, such is the adornment of a buddha-field.
The self-nature buddha-field is inherently complete and does not rely on artificial adornment; therefore, it is said that "it is not an adornment.
Because the mind is eternally pure, it is adorned even without adornment; therefore, it is said that "this is named adornment. This is the response.
Thus, one gives rise to a pure mind; this refers to what was previously described as "adornment.

The former mention of "giving rise to pure faith" was the awakening of a single thought-moment (*ekakṣaṇa*), whereas this "giving rise to a pure mind" is the cultivation of the entire body. The six perfections and myriad practices are all for the sake of cultivating this purity.
This is the primordial ground, which is itself the ultimate ground. As for the previous statement regarding non-abiding in form and so forth while practicing giving:
This refers to the non-abiding of the mind with respect to form and so forth; it subsumes all phenomena within the mind. To say "non-abiding" is more subtle.

Furthermore, while it was previously stated that "one should practice giving without abiding anywhere," here it says "one should give rise to the mind without abiding anywhere," and moreover, not clinging to the marks of giving.
That which is the state of inexhaustible purity is itself "giving rise. If there is anything to abide in, [it is not true giving].
And yet, the mind arises. This turbid and distracted mind, arising without abiding anywhere, is precisely the pure mind.
As for the arising of this mind, it is neither like withered wood or extinguished ashes, nor does it enter into a state of inert emptiness. This is the phrase: "The mind arises without abiding."
This constitutes the general purport of the entire sutra.
This treatise extracts the essential points of abiding and subduing, teaching that bodhisattvas take purity as their adornment.
When bodhisattvas cultivate the six perfections and myriad practices to assist in propagating the Buddha’s transformation, it is not that they do not adorn the buddha-fields.
However, one does not grasp at external marks as adornments. One should know that true adornment is the pure mind. It is a mind that dwells in no marks;
when the mind has nothing upon which to dwell, it is unattached in the slightest degree, and the myriad objects are crystal clear—this is purity.
It is like a single mirror facing the sky: there is nothing it does not reflect. How pure it is! If one were first to attach a single object to it, then it would no longer be empty.

If there is illumination that obscures, how can it illuminate objects? To have no place of abiding is to move from reality toward emptiness; to give rise to this mind is to produce awakening from emptiness.
This word "mind" is correct wisdom (*samyag-jñāna*); it is the true mind (*tathatā-citta*). However, if one dwells in attachment to objects, it remains hidden and does not manifest.
If the mind does not dwell [on objects], *prajñā* is vividly clear. That which gives rise to this mind manifests the fundamental.
There is the true mind; it does not arise abruptly. This phrase is the adamantine true eye, the wondrous mind of Prajñā.
Long ago, when the Sixth Patriarch heard the phrase "give rise to the mind by dwelling nowhere," he attained great enlightenment and said:
"How unexpected that self-nature is fundamentally pure! How unexpected that self-nature is fundamentally neither arising nor ceasing! How unexpected that self-nature is fundamentally..."
It is inherently complete. How unexpected that its own nature is fundamentally without movement! How unexpected that its own nature can give rise to the myriad dharmas!
A student under the gate of the Patriarchs should, from the point of "giving rise to the mind from non-abiding," realize the subtle meaning.

Lecture: It is said that the Buddha has nothing to attain. How can the various Bodhisattvas who study the Buddha’s path merely occupy themselves with adorning the Buddha-lands without seeking their own minds? Therefore, he addressed Subhūti, saying:
"If a Bodhisattva dwells within a Buddha-land and indeed performs virtuous conditions and meritorious deeds, will they thereby cause the Buddha-land to be adorned? Subhūti replied:
"No. That which the Buddha calls adornment is not the adornment of external physical marks and features.
It must be that one's mind-ground is luminous and pure, and the myriad practices are fully perfected; this is what is called adornment.
Thereupon, the Buddha followed his words and said to him: "Since the adornment of a Bodhisattva does not reside in external ornamentation, you should turn back and seek it within."
The mind should be such that within the vast expanse of the universe, it remains profoundly still and eternally empty, without a single trace of defilement;
within the inner sanctuary of the spirit, it remains tranquil and eternally settled, without a single thread of disturbance. One should give rise to such a pure mind.
One must not dwell upon the arising of the mind in response to forms, sounds, smells, tastes, tangibles, or mental phenomena. Should one dwell upon any of these, the mind can no longer be pure.
One must know that the pure mind is wondrously profound, perfectly tranquil, and does not adhere to specific locations; it fundamentally has no place of abiding.
One gives rise to this mind within non-abiding. Like a bright mirror set before one, it reflects all things as they come, and when things depart, it is empty;
naturally, it is ten times pure. What could be more magnificent than such adornment of the Pure Land?
Subhūti, suppose there were a person whose body was as large as Sumeru, the king of mountains. What do you think?
Would that body be great? Subhūti replied, "It would be very great, World-Honored One. Why is this? The Buddha has taught that what is not a body is called a 'great body.'"
Note: Sumeru is the greatest of mountains and the king of all mountains; thus it is called the "Mountain King.
How could a human body be so vast? It is merely a figurative expression, like the phrase "the seven treasures filling the great trichiliocosm.

When the preceding passage spoke of the "mind" and this one speaks of the "body," it is not a case of speaking of something external to the mind. The word "body" (shen) should be understood as the word "mind" (xin).
Observe: "Non-body" refers to the Dharma-body, which is the true mind and its original nature. That which is called the "Great Body" among non-bodies is precisely the non-abiding of the true mind;
it is sufficient to encompass the vast void and contain the sands of worlds.
Commentary: This follows from the preceding passage on the "mind arising without abiding," because it perceives that the measure of the mind is vast, pervasive, and inexhaustible.
To say that the mind has no place of abiding means that the pure mind constantly arises and the Dharma-body is perfected;
this mind is the most expansive. Thus, the Tathāgata established the Great Body (Mahākāya) as a question, and the Venerable One realized the True Mind of Non-abiding.

It pervades the entire Dharma-realm and wondrously encompasses all existence; its magnitude is equal to empty space, such that even Mount Sumeru is insufficient to serve as a metaphor for its vastness.
When the question and answer reach this point, one sees that both the body and the land are empty, and both mind and objects are transcended; thus, there is no further mention of merit and virtue.
Yet their merit is difficult to measure. Therefore, the subsequent passage proceeds to compare and evaluate such merit.
The preceding section stated that adorning Buddha-lands is not as good as purifying this mind.
Furthermore, fearing that one might mistakenly regard the physical body as great rather than realizing that the mind is great, he poses the question: "Subhūti, it is as if, for example, a person..."
"If one's body were like Sumeru, the King of Mountains, could it be called large? Subhūti answered that it would indeed be very large.
Why? Although the physical body (rūpakāya) is vast, because it is subject to arising and ceasing, it ultimately cannot be called a "large body.
When the Buddha speaks of "non-body," he refers to my own pure fundamental mind. This mind encompasses the great void and fills all phenomena.
The realms are signless and non-abiding; entering suddenly into perfect clarity is the true Dharmakāya, and this is called the Great Body.
Subhūti, suppose there were as many Ganges Rivers as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River—what do you think?
Would the sands of all those Ganges Rivers be many? Subhūti said: "Very many, World-Honored One. However, all...
“The Ganges River alone already contains countless sands; how much more so its grains! Subhūti, I now tell you this in truth:

if there were a son or daughter of good family who, with the seven treasures, filled as many trichiliocosm worlds as there are grains of sand in those Ganges Rivers and offered them as a gift, would they gain much merit? Subhūti replied, “Very much, World-Honored One. The Buddha said:

The Buddha addressed Subhūti: "If a son of good family or a daughter of good family, from within this sutra, were to receive, uphold, or even recite as little as a four-line verse for the sake of others, the merit of this would surpass the former merit."
Note: The Ganges is a river in India, the land of the West, forty *li* in circumference. Its sand is as fine as flour.

Because the Buddha frequently preached the Dharma here, it is taken as a metaphor. The phrase "sand equal to the Ganges" is an inverted construction, meaning that the Ganges is like the quantity of its sand.
It is also a term of supposition. Previously, only three thousand [great... was mentioned.
"A thousand worlds"—this expression refers to a number like that of the sands of the Ganges;
they are vast and numerous, and their measure is even more incalculable than the former, surpassing the merit of giving.

Treatise: This is the second comparison of merit. In the first comparison, because it was previously stated that both persons and phenomena are empty and all are ultimately subsumed within the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), it was said that "the Buddha-dharma all issues from this sutra" to provide an inspiration.
Below, [the text] enumerates the śrāvakas and bodhisattvas, showing that they all likewise proceed from the unconditioned dharma.
Within this, many distinctions are manifested. [The text] exhorts all bodhisattvas not to dwell in the arising of the mind, yet entrusts itself to the metaphor of the "great body" to verify this;
thus, the entire essence and great function within the pure *dharmakāya* appear simultaneously.
This is why, in the comparison of merits, each step becomes deeper than the last.
Lecture: The preceding statement that "the mind arises from non-abiding" implies that the merit of such purity is immeasurable.
Therefore, the Buddha immediately expanded upon this meaning through the practice of giving, saying: "Subhūti, the sands of the Ganges are indeed many.
Suppose there were not just one Ganges River, but as many Ganges Rivers as there are grains of sand; within all these Ganges Rivers..."
“Are those sands many or not? Subhūti replied, “They are very many. Even the Ganges Rivers alone are already numerous beyond counting; how much more so the sands within those Ganges Rivers?

The Buddha said to Subhūti, “If there were a son of good family or a daughter of good family who, with the seven treasures filling as many great trichiliocosm worlds as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River, were to give them as a gift, would they obtain [much merit]?”
"Is the merit great? Subhūti answered that it was exceedingly great.

The Buddha said, "If there are sons or daughters of good family who receive this sutra without doubt and uphold it without loss, they will certainly perceive the true nature of their own *tathatā* (suchness) and *bodhi* (enlightenment).
Furthermore, they will be able to explain the wondrous meaning of the true emptiness for others, causing people..."
When the mind-ground is opened and one clearly realizes one's own nature, one can escape saṃsāra and forever transcend birth and death;
thus, both self and others are perfected. The merit of this endures through kalpas; how could the giving of alms as numerous as the sands of the Ganges ever equal it?

Furthermore, Subhūti, wherever this sutra is spoken, even as little as a single four-line verse, you should know that this place is worthy of being honored by all the world—including its devas, humans, and asuras—as if it were a stupa or temple of the Buddha.
How much more so for those who are able to fully receive, uphold, read, and recite it? Subhūti, you should know that such persons have accomplished the most supreme and foremost rarity.
Regarding the existence of this Dharma: wherever this sutra is located, there is a Buddha, as well as his honored disciples. (Note:
"In accordance with what is taught" means that it corresponds to the entirety [of the teaching] hereafter; this refers to the meaning of the scriptural passage cited in this section.)
The place where the sutra was preached. "Worldly beings" refers to devas, humans, and asuras—namely, those of the celestial realm, the human realm, and the māra realm.

"Offerings" include such things as incense, flowers, necklaces, banners, pennants, and precious canopies. A "stūpa" is that which enshrines the Buddha’s relics; a "temple" is that which establishes images of the Buddha.
"Receiving" means comprehending its meaning, which is the wisdom of reflection (cintāmayī-prajñā). "Upholding" [refers to...]

To wear it upon one's breast without losing it is the cultivation of wisdom (*bhāvanā-mayī-prajñā*). To read in accordance with the original text is the wisdom of hearing (*śruta-mayī-prajñā*). To recite apart from the original text is also the wisdom of hearing.

If one reads and recites before having received and upheld [the teaching], the benefit realized is still shallow; once one has received and upheld it, then reading and reciting lead to a profound realization of its analogies.
The cultivation of the myriad practices is entirely subsumed within these four characters. That which can lead one toward Bodhi is called "supreme";
that which no other vehicle can equal is called "foremost"; that which does not exist in the world is called "rare. "Dharma" refers here to the Dharma of Bodhi.
Only after the Dharma has been accomplished can merit be achieved; therefore, the subsequent text speaks of "accomplishing merit."
The two characters "ruò" (若) are not empty words; rather, they are terms used to deeply praise those who have attained the foremost [realization].
"Respectable disciples" refers to the Dharma Jewel among the disciples—those worthy of respect—and the Buddha Jewel, as well as the Sangha Jewel.
Wherever the scriptures are located, there the Three Jewels are present together.
Treatise:
The preceding section spoke of the superiority of the merit of upholding this sutra; here, it further explains the reason for that superiority.

The previous two points mentioned obtaining blessings through both receiving and upholding [the sutra] as well as explaining it to others, presented together. This was done for fear that students might merely pursue [the practice] in vain.

Regarding the chapters and verses: if one merely strives for the excellence of worldly merit while failing to contemplate and cultivate the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*), then one cannot achieve fulfillment for oneself;
how then could one benefit others? Therefore, emphasis is placed on receiving and upholding [the teachings] to demonstrate the foundation of preaching the Dharma.
"Following what is preached" refers to a single section of Prajñāpāramitā; "exhausting all that can be done" refers to the entire body [of the teaching].
This is Prajñā. Those who are able to fully receive, uphold, read, and recite it possess the adamantine, profound wisdom;
there is not a single thing that does not enter within these six characters. Therein lie immeasurable meritorious practices. Where is the scripture? It is precisely within this mind.
If one is able to fully uphold and recite it, they will be able to recite this sutra from their own mind and understand the meaning of this sutra from their own mind. Self-...
The essence of the mind attains the wondrous principle of non-attachment and signlessness; with every thought, one exerts diligence and constantly cultivates the practices of a Buddha.
When this wisdom merges with that principle, wherever a scripture is found, it is as if a Buddha were present—this is what is meant by "seeing the Tathāgata in the aforementioned text.
Taking refuge and upholding [the teachings], regarding oneself as a disciple of the Mahāyāna worthy of honor, is what is meant by "shouldering the burden" in the subsequent text.
Thus spoke the Tathāgata.
To explain: how is it seen that the merit of upholding and expounding this sutra is superior? The Buddha again addressed Subhūti, saying:
"If there is someone who, according to the meaning of even a single passage of this sutra, or as little as a four-line stanza," and so forth.
One should preach the Dharma for them, causing those who listen to eliminate their deluded minds.

Then, at the place where the sutra is preached, it will naturally move the world’s devas, humans, asuras, and others to all come with reverence, as they would gaze upon and pay homage with earnest devotion to a stupa housing a relic or a temple enshrining an image.
Indeed, by following even a single verse or stanza of the teaching, one can still move the devas, nāgas, and the eight classes of beings.

If one makes offerings in this manner, how much more so for a person who is able to receive and uphold this entire sutra, internalizing it within their heart, and reading, reciting, and investigating its meaning?
One should know that such a person has, with a single mind, accomplished the Dharma of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; this is truly supreme and beyond compare. However...
It is singular and beyond compare; it is something utterly rare and unique. Wherever this scripture resides, that is where the Buddha resides.
One’s mind will remain constantly pure, and one shall attain the wondrous nature of True Suchness (Tathatā). Is this not indeed to be the eminent disciple of the Buddha’s gate?
General Explanation: From the Buddha’s statement regarding the four fruits up to this point, five sections constitute one unit.
The Buddha takes the non-thought of the four fruits and Śākyamuni’s lack of attainment as the realization of signlessness (*animitta*). Even the adornment of speech follows this signlessness.
Specifically for the sake of all bodhisattvas, he extracts the phrase "one should give rise to the mind by dwelling nowhere" and establishes it as the core principle of the Buddha’s teaching.
The essential point: the source-mind of the thousand sages lies within this single phrase. Furthermore, it is said that the measure of "generating the mind without abiding" is most vast;
its supreme merit lies solely in upholding this sutra. Having reached this point, Subhūti has already attained wondrous realization;
therefore, in the following text, he directly requests the name of the sutra and the method for its upholding.
At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying, “World-Honored One, what should this sutra be named?
How should we uphold it? The Buddha told Subhūti, “This sutra is named the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā*;
by this name you should uphold it. Why is this so? Subhūti, when the Buddha speaks of the *Prajñāpāramitā*, it is [as follows]...”
That which is not the perfection of wisdom is called the perfection of wisdom. Subhūti, what do you think?
Has the Tathāgata preached any dharma? Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, the Tathāgata has preached nothing" (the ancient text lacks the phrase "is called the perfection of wisdom").

**Commentary:** All that the Buddha spoke constitutes the *sūtras*. First, he is referred to as the one who speaks words and phrases; next, he is referred to as the Dharma; and finally, he is referred to as the *sūtra*.
At this point, the request is made to establish a title for the *sūtra*. This is because, in order to understand the meaning and intent, one must first know the name of the *sūtra*.

By requesting that the name be revealed, it is hoped that there will be no lack of a method for upholding and maintaining it. The name of the Dharma is Prajñā; it illuminates and perceives that all phenomena (*dharmas*) are empty.
The Dharma is metaphorized as the vajra, specifically referring to the single, true, and indestructible reality.

The Buddha bestowed upon it the name "Prajñā" (Wisdom) and further added the two characters "Vajra" (Diamond/Thunderbolt) to demonstrate its ultimate hardness and sharpness, such that it does not consort with any of the myriad dharmas.
Thus, all things are simultaneously empty, yet all things are simultaneously complete; this is precisely what it means to reach the other shore.
This entire True Scripture is fully contained within these seven characters. To uphold these names is to uphold the whole scripture; one must not add a single redundant word.
Since the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is fundamentally empty and there is nothing to which one can cling, it is said that "it is not. Within this [negation], there is the truth.
Awakening is the luminosity of the myriad phenomena; therefore, it is called "this name.

Furthermore, fearing that upon hearing the name of the sutra one might fail to recognize one's own mind and instead merely cling to the fabricated form, he questions him again. Yet, Subhūti has already realized within "that which is not Prajñā" that there is no dharma that can be spoken.
Commentary: Here, the Buddha specifically reveals the title of the sutra; this is the "eye-opening" point of this entire golden scripture.
From the preceding discussion on subduing and abiding, he had not yet explicitly spoken of Prajñā. Within this interval, he exhausts the mark of saving sentient beings by means of saving them;
he exhausts the mark of giving by means of giving; he exhausts the mark of the body by means of seeing the Buddha; and he exhausts the mark of dharmas by means of pure faith.
Thus firm and thus fierce, it is entirely the wisdom of *prajñā*. Like a diamond (*vajra*), it is capable of severing;
for it is the pure, luminous, true wisdom of the fundamental mind, which remains unchanging amidst conditions.
It can destroy and sever all afflictions (*kleśa*) while itself being indestructible by anything—this is the Diamond Prajñā. What is taught in this sutra is direct...
This points to the essence of the mind. It is the method of severing all delusive conditions and attaining the other shore through wisdom (*prajñā*).
Now, *prajñā* is a single point of numinous light upon the pure essence of the human mind; it is free from all marks and is identical with all dharmas.
Throughout the entire earth, there is not a single dharma that is the place where Prajñā dwells;

nor is there a single dharma that is not the place where Prajñā emits light. "Neither being nor non-being"—this directly causes the practitioner who upholds it to leave not even a single trace of a word within their breast.
Lecture: Upon hearing this most rare and extraordinary Dharma, Subhūti understood its ultimate destination as soon as he beheld the pointing finger;

he then resolved to uphold it and requested that the name of the sutra be established. He addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, by upholding and preaching this sutra, one accomplishes a rare and extraordinary dharma.
I do not know by what name this sutra should be titled, nor how we should uphold it. The Buddha—
He said: "This sutra should be named the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā*.

This is because those who clarify this sutra possess wisdom as firm and sharp as a diamond (*vajra*), which cuts through external delusions and leads directly to the other shore of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
You should uphold it by this name. How, then, should you uphold it?"
As for what the Buddha called "Prajñāpāramitā," its nature as wondrous enlightenment is as profound and still as the great void.

Since its essence is fundamentally non-existent, how could there be a name for it? The Tathāgata, fearing that people might fall into the view of annihilationism, was compelled to provisionally designate it by the name "Prajñāpāramitā.
True nature has always been thus; what further dharma could there be?
"Subhūti, have I taught any dharma? Subhūti, knowing that all dharmas are fundamentally empty, responded by confirming:
"The Tathāgata has taught that all dharmas are empty; what is there to be taught?"
"Subhūti, what do you think? Is the amount of all the minute particles of dust in a trichiliocosm great?
Subhūti replied, "It is very great, World-Honored One. "Subhūti, those minute particles of dust spoken of by the Tathāgata are not minute particles;
they are called 'minute particles. The world spoken of by the Tathāgata is not a world; it is called a 'world.'"
Commentary: "Dust particles" refers to the eighty-four thousand afflictions (*kleśa*). "Worlds" refers to the world of sentient beings.
All the dust particles within the three-thousandfold great thousandfold world represent the boundlessness of sentient beings and the inexhaustibility of their afflictions.
To be able to cultivate the practice of non-characteristic and non-attachment through *prajñā*, and thereby comprehend deluded thoughts and afflictions—this is [the path].

Because the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is pure, it is said that "it is not atoms. Because delusion is realized as truth, and both truth and delusion are extinguished, it is said that "this is called atoms.
When the nature is free from defilement (*kleśa*), it is the world of the Buddhas; when the nature possesses defilement, it is the world of sentient beings.
Because all deluded thoughts are realized as profoundly empty and quiescent, it is said that "it is not a world. Thus one attains realization.
The Dharma-body universally perceives all lands within atoms, and its adaptive manifestations are without limit; therefore, it is called a "world-system.
*Commentary:* This demonstrates that the atom-like worlds are all empty, thereby revealing the function of Prajñā—namely, the Prajñā of Contemplative Observation (*vipaśyanā-prajñā*).
If one views them through the lens of these atom-like worlds, then the myriad phenomena fill the eyes, appearing as a dense array of phenomenal realms. However, if one views them through...
If one does not view it through the realm of sensory objects, then there is a single path of empty leisure—true emptiness and true stillness.

What is called "quiescent extinction and vacuous spirit" manifests its forms by relying upon the myriad phenomena; though illusory scenes stretch out in every direction, they return to the single nature to merge with the truth.

Indeed, the light of the *prajñā* mind encompasses the thousand worlds in its vastness and penetrates into the finest motes of dust; thus, throughout the worlds of the ten directions, there is nothing that is not [this].
It is also one's own radiance. The Buddha said to Mañjuśrī: "To be in the world yet detached from the world, to be amidst the dust yet detached from the dust—this is the ultimate Dharma;
it is the state of mind that is neither dust nor realm."
The Buddha said to Subhūti: "In a trichiliocosm, are all the atoms of dust many?
Subhūti replied that they were exceedingly many. The Buddha said: "What the Tathāgata calls 'all the atoms of dust' is originally an illusory and false thing.
The treasury of numinous emptiness is a vast space, pure and transparent; it is not composed of atoms of dust."
That which can be defiled is therefore not a literal atom; it is merely given the provisional name "atom.
When the Tathāgata speaks of the world, it is originally not something inherently existing within my mind.
When the ground of the mind is vast and open, pure and free from flaw or stain, this is precisely the supramundane dharma. It cannot be confined by the world; therefore, it is not the world. Rather—
"Empty names are what we call the world.
Subhūti, what do you think? Can the Tathāgata be seen by means of the thirty-two marks? No, World-Honored One;
the Tathāgata cannot be seen by means of the thirty-two marks. Why is this? The Tathāgata has said that the thirty-two..."
The two marks are, in fact, no-marks; this is called the thirty-two marks. (Note:
The thirty-two marks refer to the adornment and excellence of the entire body; this is the Buddha of the Form Body (*rūpakāya*).

"Seeing the Tathāgata" refers to the Dharma Body (*dharmakāya*); when one contemplates that these marks are fundamentally illusory, there is nothing to point out or describe, yet this does not hinder [the realization].)
Marks are themselves marklessness; therefore it is said that they are "not body-marks. Contemplating the original truth of their nature, every dust mote is wondrous awakening.
Thus, marklessness does not preclude being marks; therefore it is said, "These are called the thirty-two marks."
Treatise: These words state that the marks are not identical to the marks, thereby revealing the essence of Prajñā—namely, the Prajñā of True Reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa-prajñā*).
The previous statement that "the realms of dust are not realms of dust" refers to departing from illusion to return to emptiness;

this present statement that "the bodily marks are not bodily marks" refers to realizing reality through the very nature of emptiness. One should know that the thirty-two marks are merely the *rūpakāya* Tathāgata.
There is another, the True Nature Tathāgata, which is neither form nor emptiness, transcending all myriad phenomena, unchanging and indestructible, entirely subsumed within the One Reality.
Therefore it is said: "This appearance is itself non-appearance. To recognize this non-appearance is what is called the true appearance.
The Discourse: The Buddha asked Subhūti, "Can the Tathāgata be perceived by means of the thirty-two marks?
Subhūti replied, "Although the marks of the Tathāgata are supreme, wondrous, and extraordinary, they should not be sought through form and color. Why is this?
It is because the 'marks' spoken of by the Tathāgata are not the true marks; his wondrous essence is suchness (*tathatā*), serene and profound."
"Perpetual quiescence is the fundamental mind of all Buddhas; this is called the thirty-two marks.

Subhūti, if there were a son of good family or a daughter of good family who were to give away their body and life as numerous as the sands of the Ganges in acts of charity, yet another person were to receive, uphold, or even recite a single four-line verse from this sutra and explain it to others—"
The merit thereof is exceedingly great.

*Commentary:* The Buddha first compared the gift of the jewels of a great trichiliocosm to the excellence of this sutra; next, he compared the gift of jewels as numerous as the sands of the Ganges to the excellence of this sutra.

Both of these were external wealth (*bāhya-dhana*). Reaching this point, he speaks of the giving of one’s body and life, which constitutes internal wealth (*ādhyātma-dhana*). Compared [to the former], [the latter is superior].
Although the gift of material wealth is excellent, it remains entirely within the realm of tainted causes and effects; it does not equal the superior merit of upholding this sutra.
This serves as the beginning of the subsequent comparison between physical life and [the merit of the Dharma].
Treatise: This is the third comparison of merit. To receive and uphold [this teaching] is the cause of the Dharma-body;
therefore, this merit is the most preeminent. Regarding this section of the sūtra, it begins with "receiving and upholding" (*parigraha*) and concludes with "upholding" (*dhāraṇa*);

one should pay close attention to this. For one who is truly able to receive and uphold acts in accordance with the nature (*dharmatā*), manifesting from the fundamental mind—there is nothing that is not so.
This is the entire body of the Vajra.

its wondrous function is without fixed direction and cannot be called empty. Such is the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*): true emptiness and wondrous function. Thus, one should practice giving without dwelling on anything.
Furthermore, regarding those whose minds dwell upon dharmas: while they have not yet purified the six sense objects within the causal stage, they believe that practicing goodness can produce merit.
They regard the Buddha-way as mysterious and spiritually responsive, yet they have not even dreamed of the wisdom that awakens to the fundamental measure of humanity.

If this mind flows entirely from a single expanse of compassion, welcoming opportunities to guide others well and saving beings through successive acts, so that sentient beings in the five turbidities may all ascend to the other shore—this is the thorough penetration of the source and its stream, where the light of the nature illuminates all;
this is precisely the benefit of giving. One attains True Suchness through the purity of the mind, and the purity of the mind arises from non-abiding.
The Dharma does not abide; it exists by virtue of wisdom, and wisdom arises from hearing the sutras. One should know that this sutra possesses supreme merit;
therefore, it must be praised in order to manifest it for future generations.
The Master said: "What the Tathāgata has spoken as the Prajñāpāramitā is entirely the unsurpassed Bodhi.
It is the realization of one's original nature—true and not false, real and not empty. Its words are suchness (*tathatā*) and do not change;
they are not deceptive speech, nor are they extraordinary doctrines. It is by means of this that the Tathāgata attained this Prajñā."

As for the Dharma, it is simply emptiness. There is no mental dharma that performs the emptying. If one takes the Dharma to be real, its true essence is empty and still, fundamentally lacking any reality.
If one takes the Dharma to be void, its wondrous function is boundless and has no fixed direction, yet it is not void either.
Therefore, a practicing bodhisattva should realize true emptiness and ought not to dwell upon or become attached to anything when performing acts of giving.
If one performs giving with a mind attached to phenomena, then the four marks have not yet been emptied;

this constitutes the obscuration of ignorance, like a person in a dark room who is dimly sighted and sees nothing. If, however, one performs giving with a mind free from attachment, [the four marks are emptied].

Then, one will become perfectly enlightened regarding the Tathāgata, penetrating all things with unimpeded clarity, like a person who possesses eyes, or as if the bright sun has appeared in the sky, allowing one to see all manner of forms.

If, in future generations, there are sons or daughters of good family who can receive, uphold, read, and recite this sutra, they will immediately and suddenly awaken to true emptiness, thereby reaching the stage of Bodhi-awakening and becoming the Tathāgata of their own inherent nature. This is the Buddha.
With the eye of wisdom, one knows all and sees all; how could one not thereby accomplish immeasurable and boundless merit?
Subhūti, if there were good sons or good daughters who, during the first part of the day, [offered] bodies as numerous as the sands of the Ganges...
If one were to give away as many bodies as there are grains of sand in the Ganges during the midday portion of a day,

and likewise give away as many bodies as there are grains of sand in the Ganges during the afternoon portion of that same day— thus giving away one's body for immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of kalpas—

and if there were another person who, upon hearing this sutra, believed it with a mind free from opposition, their merit would surpass the former; how much more so if they were to copy, receive, and uphold it?
To uphold, read, recite, and explain it to others.
*Annotation:* "The first day," "the middle day," and "the latter day" refer to a single day, meaning the three periods of morning, midday, and evening.
"Sands of the Ganges" expresses its great quantity; "immeasurable kalpas" expresses its long duration. Both serve as metaphors. This is what the Buddha meant by "renunciation."
The "giving of one's body" is not something that truly exists [in a literal sense]; it is the Confucian teaching of "diminishing oneself to benefit others.
"Faith" refers to the aforementioned purity of faith. "Not being contrary" refers to the aforementioned state of not being startled, not being terrified, and not being afraid;
this is to be in accord with Prajñā and to follow it with a single mind. Hearing the sutra with faith and having no opposition or contrariness is simply a matter of the ears.

The faculty of the body is superior; how much more so when the six faculties are pure! Furthermore, there are those who excel even further: for one who writes it down, the faculty of the body is superior as it embodies the Prajñā;
for one who receives and upholds it, the faculty of the mind is superior as it embodies the Prajñā;

for one who reads and recites it, the faculty of the tongue is superior as it embodies the Prajñā. These constitute the merit of self-benefit. As for explaining it to others, this is the benefit of others.
On His Virtues. Treatise:
This is the fourth comparison of merit. Although one may sacrifice body and life, it cannot lead to the realization of one’s nature;

it remains a cause for out-flowing karma (*āsrava*). By hearing this sutra and gaining faith, one suddenly perceives one’s own nature (*svabhāva*) and practices with single-minded resolve. Furthermore...
There is no regression. This person attains the merit of *prajñā*, which far surpasses the merit of giving one's life.
Writing it down, upholding it, and explaining it flows forth from the light of *prajñā*. These words and letters proclaim the Buddha’s teachings on his behalf;
they are not merely words set upon paper. One may compare them by interpreting the meaning according to the text.

The Buddha said: "Suppose there were sons or daughters of good family who, for the duration of a single day, were to give away their lives as many times as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River, and continue doing so for immeasurable kalpas—how could the resulting merit and retribution ever be fully described?"

However, such [merit] can only receive the stubborn worldly blessings. If there is someone who hears this sutra, believes it in their heart, and does not contradict its teaching, their merit is already superior to the merit of sacrificing one's body;
how much more so for those who copy its chapters and verses, investigate its words, uphold, read, and recite it to understand its principles, and furthermore, bestow this sutra upon others?
To explain its meaning is not merely to clarify one's own nature; it also teaches others to each perceive their own nature.
When the roots of goodness are fully matured, the benefit is inexhaustible. How could such merit have any limit?
General Explanation: From "He himself deeply understood the meaning and intent" up to this point, there are seven sections forming one unit.

After Subhūti heard the name of the Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, he personally recounted his realization and understanding. He praised those who believe in the sūtra for giving rise to the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) and for being free from signs (*animitta*), deeming them the most rare and extraordinary.
Consequently, the Buddha stated that the Prajñā of the true mark is the foremost among the six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*).
Furthermore, taking patience and giving as examples to illustrate the rest, he teaches that practice arises from understanding.
Within each of the six *pāramitās*, one should generate the mind of awakening while remaining detached from all signs (*lakṣaṇa*), thereby benefiting sentient beings.

This is encompassed by the essential tenets of Prajñā: being "without reality" and "without falsehood. "Without reality" means that all phenomena are empty; this is precisely what is meant by being detached from signs. Without...
"Emptiness" refers precisely to the true, eternally abiding reality-mark (*dharmatā*). This is the wondrous realm of *bodhi*.

Furthermore, by using the analogy of entering a dark place to clarify that the mark of illumination has no fixed location, he again evaluates merit once more to demonstrate that the person of wisdom who possesses *prajñā* achieves both [self-benefit and benefit for others], something that cannot be attained even by sacrificing one's life.
Subhūti, to speak of it in brief, this sutra possesses inconceivable, immeasurable, and boundless merit.
It was taught by the Tathāgata for those who have set out upon the Great Vehicle, and for those who have set out upon the Supreme Vehicle.
If there be anyone who can receive, uphold, read, recite, and extensively explain it to others, the Tathāgata fully knows that person; the Tathāgata fully sees that person. All such individuals...
They shall attain the accomplishment of immeasurable, incomparable, boundless, and inconceivable merit;
such persons as these shall indeed bear the burden of the Tathāgata’s *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. Why is this?
Subhūti, if those who delight in inferior dharmas cling to the view of a self, the view of a person, the view of a sentient being, or the view of a life-span, then...
Subhūti, wherever this sutra may be found—whether it be heard, received, read, recited, or explained to others—that place should be honored by all the world, including its devas, humans, and asuras.
You should know that such a place is itself a stupa; it should be revered, saluted, and circumambulated, and one should scatter flowers and incense upon it.

"Abode. (Note: "Essential" [yào] refers to the fundamental principle [zōng]. Speech must ultimately return to this principle. This sutra is the *prajñāpāramitā* of the true reality (*bhūtatathatā*) as elucidated within its words and letters.
"Vehicle" (*yāna*) refers to a carriage; it takes the sense of the turning of the Wheel of Dharma and universal penetration. "Mahāyāna" refers to the Bodhisattva.
It is a vehicle; it is the Supreme Vehicle, the Buddha-vehicle. The Sixth Patriarch said: "In the Dharma there are no three vehicles;
it is the human mind that possesses degrees of difference. To see, hear, recite, and chant is the Small Vehicle. To awaken to the Dharma and understand its meaning is the Middle Vehicle.
To practice according to the Dharma is the Great Vehicle. When all phenomena are fully understood, all practices are complete, and one is unstained by anything—this is to be free from all dharmas."
Characteristics. "Nothing to be attained" refers to the Supreme Vehicle (*agrayāna*). "To give rise to" means that the practitioner arouses the bodhicitta.
"Supreme merit" refers to the merits inherent within the sutra itself; "inferior" refers to the merits accomplished by others.
"To shoulder and bear" means to directly take the Buddha-dharma upon one's own shoulders. "Inferior teachings" refers to those of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*). [End of] previous section.

To speak of the "four characteristics" (lakṣaṇa) refers to the six sense objects (*viṣaya*); this is still coarse. To speak here of the "four views" (*dṛṣṭi*) refers to the six sense faculties (*indriya*);
this is somewhat more subtle. Furthermore, deluded view is the very root of deluded characteristics. What was previously called "stūpas and temples" refers to places where the sutras were preached;
this refers to places where the sutras currently exist; each has its own distinction. "Various flowers and incense" refers to precious blossoms and exquisite fragrances.
Treatise: This section generally summarizes the preceding text, stating that this sutra is subtle and profound;

only those who have resolved to attain the Great Vehicle (Mahāyāna) are able to shoulder the burden of the Buddha-dharma. To resolve for the Great Vehicle, the Supreme Vehicle, is precisely to resolve for *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Bodhisattvas are those who have already resolved for the Supreme Vehicle, while virtuous men and women are those capable of so resolving.

Those of the Supreme Vehicle are sentient beings who have not yet set out upon the Supreme Vehicle; yet those who have not yet set out upon the Supreme Vehicle are, in reality, those capable of setting out upon it.
The Tathāgata, entrusting himself to the bodhisattvas, speaks for the sake of those who have already set out upon the Supreme Vehicle.
This is specifically for those who have not yet generated the aspiration for the Supreme Vehicle (anuttarayāna) to inspire them to do so. As for "the one who bears the burden":

since Bodhi is fundamentally rooted in the Tathāgata, this demonstrates the core principle of the transmission and reception of the True Dharma (saddharma). The Tathāgata’s protective mindfulness and entrustment are solely directed toward seeking such a person to bear the burden.
The concluding statement that "this sutra contains the entire body of the Buddha" means that wherever it is circulated, that very place is...
The Dharma-body is eternally abiding; it encompasses the meaning of holding this sutra with folded hands, being perfectly complete and all-pervasive, thereby fulfilling the aspirations of all people.
To speak of Subhūti: in brief, this sutra cannot be conceived by the mind nor discussed by the mouth.
One may gauge the capacity of a person by their disposition; this [teaching] possesses boundless merit.
For this reason, the Tathāgata does not lightly preach it to others, but preaches it only for those of great capacity who have resolved to attain Bodhicitta.

If there should be anyone who receives, upholds, recites, and reads it, and explains it extensively to others, the Tathāgata knows them all and sees them all, as well as their spiritual efficacy and virtuous conduct.
All these can be accomplished. Such a person is able to shoulder the Dharma of the Tathāgata’s unsurpassed bodhi within a single body;
how could those who delight in lesser dharmas be compared to them?

For those who delight in lesser dharmas are deluded by non-Buddhist paths and cannot escape the private attachments of views such as the self and persons (*pudgala-dṛṣṭi*). Regarding true nature (*tathatā*), they remain utterly ignorant. Therefore—
They are unable to hear, receive, read, recite, or explain it for others. They do not know that this sutra universally reveals all things, being most subtle and most wondrous.
Subhūti, wherever this scripture exists, all the worlds—gods, humans, and asuras—will make offerings to it. You should know that such a place is the very body of the Tathāgata.
The precious stupa of Śāriputra enables those far and near to gaze upon it with reverence and single-minded solemnity;
to prostrate themselves with their five limbs touching the ground; and for the great assembly to circumambulate it in taking refuge.

By scattering various flowers and incense at the place where this sutra is upheld, one’s offerings may be said to reach their ultimate perfection. Truly so for those who uphold and recite it with faith.
They will then be able to shoulder the burden of Bodhi. Furthermore, Subhūti,
if a son of good family or a daughter of good family receives, upholds, reads, and recites this sutra, yet is treated with contempt by others,

it is because their karmic offenses from previous lives— which would have caused them to fall into the evil realms— have been exhausted by the fact that they are now being treated with contempt by people in this life.
The sinful karma of previous lives shall be immediately extinguished, and one shall attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
*Annotation:* "Being despised" refers to illness and poverty; it includes minor afflictions and humiliations, as well as major ones such as death.
"Previous lives" refers to past incarnations. In reality, turning from evil in the past toward goodness in the present constitutes a transformation within a single lifetime;

this too is called a "life. The Sixth Patriarch takes "previous life" and "present life" to signify the preceding thought-moment and the succeeding thought-moment, which also applies to the evil realms—the three paths of hell, hungry ghosts, and animals. Entering the gate of merit, then... [the previous]... first...
The karmic offenses of the world are extinguished; by entering the gate of wisdom, one attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. Commentary:
