The preceding statement spoke of receiving blessings through upholding [the teaching], while this statement speaks of extinguishing offenses through upholding it. The former was spoken for the sake of the Mahāyāna regarding its merits;
this is spoken for the sake of the Hīnayāna regarding its retributive fruits. The discourse on retributive fruits is most capable of moving the worldly mind.

Therefore, I shall speak of this briefly. When people see those who uphold this sutra suffer misfortunes in their present lives, being subjected to insults, abuse, and contempt, they conclude that it is of no benefit and develop a sense of discouragement.
Thus, the Buddha spoke of cause and effect to refute such views; it was precisely to strengthen the resolve of those practicing the Dharma.
"Lay down the butcher’s knife, and you can become a Buddha on the spot"—this refers to the boundless suffering [of the hells].
The sea: turning one's head, one immediately ascends [the shore]. Holding the sutras, one realizes the nature; changing the bones and shedding the womb.
This is what is meant by "Do not cast yourself outside the kiln of the Creator; widely ferry across the boundless great Dharma-boat."
Lecture: Regarding the recitation of this sutra, one ought to be honored by devas and humans, yet one cannot avoid being treated with contempt by people.
Few do not consider such recitation to be of no benefit. Therefore, the Buddha said:

"Subhūti, if a person can uphold and recite this sutra, they are carrying the burden of the True Dharma on their shoulders and should be honored by devas and humans. If, on the contrary, they are treated with contempt by people..."
This lowliness must stem from great karmic offenses committed in previous lives, when greed, anger, and delusion were indulged and the body, speech, and mind were unrestrained;

one ought to have fallen into the three evil realms. Now, by relying on the merit of upholding this sutra, one receives only the punishment of being treated with contempt, while the karmic offenses of former lives are immediately eliminated.
How much more so now that the awakened mind has arisen—offenses are extinguished and blessings are produced; thus, the cause is removed and the fruit follows.
"Subhūti, you shall presently attain unsurpassed bodhi.
Subhūti, I recall that in the past, during immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas before the time of the Buddha Dīpaṃkara,
I encountered eight hundred and forty *koṭi-nayuta* Buddhas, all of whom I served and made offerings to, never letting my efforts go to waste."

Furthermore, Subhūti, if there should be a son of good family or a daughter of good family who, in the final age at the end of time, is able to receive, uphold, read, and recite this sutra, the merit they thereby obtain would surpass the merit of making offerings to all the Buddhas whom I have served;
it would not be equal to even a hundredth part, nor a thousandth, nor ten million-billionth part, nor even could it be reached by calculation, number, or analogy.
Subhūti, if a son of good family or a daughter of good family, in the future...
If I were to fully describe the merit obtained by those who receive, uphold, read, and recite this sutra in the final age,
some who hear it might have their minds become deranged, fall into doubt, and fail to believe. Subhūti, you should know that the meaning of this sutra is inconceivable,
and its karmic fruition is likewise inconceivable.
Note: *Asaṃkhyeya* is translated into Chinese as "innumerable" (*wúyāngshù*). *Kalpa* is equivalent to a "world-age.
"Before the Buddha Dīpaṃkara" means prior to encountering the Buddha Dīpaṃkara. *Upapanna* (here rendered as *zhí*) means "to encounter. *Nayuta* is translated into Chinese as "ten million.

"Detailed explanation" (*jùshuō*) refers to a thorough account. Regarding the "detailed explanation of merits," it is as described in the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra*. It is "extreme" (*jí*)... [text continues].
"A land of bliss" refers to the accomplishment of such adornments of merit. "Madness and confusion" means delusion and falsehood.
"Doubt and suspicion" means wavering and perplexity. "Retribution" means the manifestation of karmic results.
Treatise: This fifth section compares and measures merit, summarizing the inconceivable nature of the virtues of upholding this sutra.
The Buddha further deprecates himself in order to manifest the merit of receiving and upholding it.

He states that one who makes offerings by serving immeasurable Buddhas is not equal to one who receives and upholds [this sutra] by bearing the burden of even a single Tathāgata; this refers to making offerings.
It is not that this is not for those who receive and uphold it, nor is it that the Buddha was inferior to people of the末法 (mofa, final dharma) age. The merits have been fully explained;
there are many instances of responsive miracles and karmic retributions. For this reason, they easily give rise to madness, confusion, and doubt in people.
Nevertheless, the karmic retribution is ultimately inconceivable. The Buddha did not calculate the retribution, but rather spoke with utmost emphasis of the excellence of this sutra, wishing to—

"Resolute persons" refers to those who believe and accept [the teaching]. The final section is the summary. These two phrases represent the meaning of the sutra; furthermore, they constitute the "knot within the knot.

The Buddha said: "Just as I, throughout incalculable kalpas prior to the time of Dīpaṃkara Buddha, encountered eight hundred and forty thousand *koṭi-nayuta* Buddhas appearing in the world, and served them all with total devotion without ever flagging."
I have followed [the teachings] without opposition; there has not been a single moment spent in vain. My service to the various Buddhas has been as extensive as this.

If, in a future age, there should be those who uphold this sutra and perceive their own original nature, thereby attaining eternal liberation from saṃsāra, then when one compares the merit of such people with the merit of my offerings to the Buddhas, it would not even equal a hundred-thousand-million-billionth part, nor can it be calculated by any number.

The vastness of these many parables does not equal even a single fraction of the merit gained from upholding this sutra. If I were to describe in full detail the merit obtained by good sons and daughters who, during the age of the final dharma, receive, uphold, read, and recite it— (Aligned with the source structure:

...the vastness of these many parables does not equal even a single fraction of the merit gained from upholding this sutra. If I were to describe in full detail the merit obtained by good sons and daughters who, during the age of the final dharma, receive, uphold, read, and recite it—
Those of inferior faculties, upon hearing this, will give rise to deluded and false thoughts; otherwise, they will harbor doubts and fail to believe, surely regarding my words as mere exaggeration.
You should know that the essential meaning of this sutra and the karmic rewards of its merit are both beyond the reach of thought and cannot be discussed by the mouth.

General Explanation: From this point onward, the essential points are summarized. These three sections constitute one unit, collectively concluding the preceding text by stating that the excellence of this sutra lies in its signlessness (*animitta*).

If a person can distance themselves from signs, resolve their mind [on enlightenment], uphold, and widely expound this teaching, how vast is the difference between them and those who delight in inferior dharmas—like the gap between heaven and earth!
Such a person will accomplish merit, shoulder the burden of the Tathāgata, and [be freed from] transgressions.
Karma is eliminated, and one attains perfect enlightenment. How could this be equaled by making offerings to the various Buddhas?
Hereafter, all praise ceases; therefore, it is concluded with the term "inconceivable.

From the beginning of this chapter, Subhūti’s question regarding abiding and subduing the mind, and the Buddha’s demonstration of the principle of signlessness, have already made the meaning of the sutra perfectly clear. Following this—

In response to Subhūti’s inquiry regarding true faith and his request for the name of the sutra, [the Buddha] expressed the wish that sentient beings in future generations might give rise to the mark of reality and realize the signless.
Yet, the Tathāgata, according to the capacities of beings, pointed out that the essential point is to teach people to give rise to a pure mind;

only then can they realize bodhi. The final section offers an extreme praise of the excellence of the merit of upholding and expounding [this teaching], thereby strengthening people's pure faith and causing them to abide [in it].

The meaning of "descending" [into the world] concludes here; this constitutes the entirety of the first fascicle of the sutra. From below, the text merely reiterates and clarifies the intent of the preceding section.
That compassion is so profound and weighty as to not tire of repeating itself three times is certainly not redundant exposition.
*Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, Volume I; *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, Volume II. Commentary: Dayuan states:
"The first half of the text requires people to leave behind appearances in order to see the Buddha; the second half requires people..."

He thoroughly penetrates the selflessness of all phenomena. The Awakening of Faith states: "The first half of the volume exclusively discusses *prajñā*, while the second half clarifies the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*);
this is the ultimate reality of true *prajñā*. Some say that the former [section] addresses coarse attachments.

The latter statement concerns subtle grasping, while the former was taught for those who have first resolved their minds toward enlightenment (*bodhicitta*). This is detailed in the treatises on the generation of the mind;

the latter, however, is taught for those who have already generated that mind, stating directly that there is no mind to be generated. This extends to the section where Subhūti asks his question once again.
Daiyuan raised doubts regarding the repetition and again submitted his previous request.
Ruru Jushi considered this to be the initiation of a new line of inquiry rather than a re-presentation of a prior request. Various discussions ensued, yet no definitive conclusion was reached.
It is not understood why Subhūti, having already realized the essential meaning upon hearing what the Buddha had said, requested once more that [the teaching] be halted. This was because...

For the sake of the good men and women of the final age who have not yet been able to receive the Buddha’s words directly, they inquire about the method for generating the bodhicitta, wishing for the Buddha to establish a single dharma to universally instruct all sentient beings.
Therefore, the Buddha tells them that, in reality, there is no dharma whatsoever for generating the bodhicitta.

If one carefully examines the purport of the sutra, it seems appropriate to understand it in this way; for in the subsequent sections, [the Buddha] will take what was left unexplained in the preceding chapter...

The meaning of "exhaustion" (the ultimate limit) is reiterated and clarified again and again. When Subhūti further inquires about faith and further inquires about non-attainment, it is all for the purpose of preaching the Dharma for sentient beings of the末代 (final age).

Furthermore, based on the intent of the four-line verse beginning with "Whatever phenomena there may be," the Buddha reiterates this with two additional verses. The means by which he brings sentient beings to *parinirvāṇa* are vast and great indeed.

At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One, how should a son of good family or a daughter of good family who has resolved upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* abide? How should they subdue their minds? The Buddha told Subhūti:
“As for those sons of good family or daughters of good family who have resolved upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*...”
One should give rise to this thought: "I should bring all sentient beings to parinirvāṇa;
yet, after having brought all sentient beings to parinirvāṇa, not a single sentient being has actually been brought to parinirvāṇa. Why is this?
Subhūti, if a bodhisattva possesses the mark of a self, the mark of a person, the mark of a sentient being, or the mark of a life-span, they are not a bodhisattva. For what reason? Subhūti...
"Subhūti, there is no dharma whatsoever that gives rise to the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
[Commentary: The phrase "giving rise to such a mind" flows directly through the following three phrases without pausing;
the three phrases beginning with "I should bring them to extinction" all refer to this very mind. What was previously stated, "I shall cause all to be brought to extinction," manifests its power.

"This one says, 'I should bring about parinirvāṇa,' pointing to his vow. The previous statement, 'I shall bring immeasurable and boundless sentient beings to parinirvāṇa,' indicates the vastness of its scope.
This one says, 'Having brought sentient beings to parinirvāṇa,' indicating the spiritual efficacy of the merit.

The previous statement, 'In truth, there are no sentient beings to be brought to parinirvāṇa,' demonstrates equality in general. This one says, 'Not a single sentient being has been brought to parinirvāṇa,' subtly expressing the total forgetting of all."

This is a single point. Throughout this entire section, the meaning has already been explained in the preceding text; however, only in the final sentence is the phrase "in reality there is no dharma" explicitly set forth.
These four characters should be emphasized, for they not only reveal the essential purport of this specific section but also serve as a structural outline for the second half of the fascicle.
Treatise: This section explains that Subhūti, for the sake of sentient beings in the final age, requested the Tathāgata to remain and not enter extinction.
He expressed the intent that, in reality, there is no such thing as the parinirvāṇa of sentient beings, thereby demonstrating that the dharma of generating the bodhicitta is non-existent.

While the various bodhisattvas in the preceding fascicle personally received the Buddha’s teaching and had already realized the principle of being free from marks (*lakṣaṇa*), he specifically feared that sentient beings in the final age would be unable to do so personally.

Having heard the Buddha’s words, Subhūti asked this question because he realized that the Tathāgata possesses a single dharma by which he instructs sentient beings on how to subdue and abide [the mind].
Thus, as the tone differs from the previous statement, the phrasing is slightly different. Subhūti questioned him again as before.
The Buddha answered as before, adding the phrase: "In truth, there is no dharma that gives rise to the resolve [for awakening].
Seeing that even the mind that gives rise to the resolve is non-existent, how much more so the mind that abides or the mind that subdues? How could there be any further dharma?
Subhūti’s mind seeking the Dharma had not yet been transformed; therefore, the Buddha directly severed it at its very root by saying, "In truth, there is no dharma," and spoke of "giving rise to..."

Awakening is fundamentally without dharmas. From this point until the phrase "the characteristic of non-arising dharmas," all serves to cite preceding text to substantiate the subsequent meaning, thereby clarifying the significance of generating the mind of awakening through the absence of dharmas.
Lecture: At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying: "Regarding the purport of signlessness, the bodhisattvas have already received your instructions.
However, I fear that in the final age, there may be sons and daughters of good family who have not yet personally received the Buddha's teaching.
For those who have resolved upon the mind of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, how should they abide in that mind? How should they subdue their delusions?"
Reflect on this. The Buddha said: "You who have already resolved to attain perfect enlightenment should give rise to such a mind that transcends and realizes [the state of] all sentient beings.
You should uplift all sentient beings, extinguishing their deluded thoughts and transforming them.
Though you bring sentient beings to parinirvāṇa until all have become Buddhas, there is not a single sentient being who has actually been brought to parinirvāṇa."
This is simply because sentient beings save themselves and liberate themselves; I have no merit in this. Why is this?

For to harbor a mind that seeks extinction and liberation is itself to be attached to signs (*nimitta*). If a bodhisattva possesses the signs of a self, a person, a multitude, or a life-span, they certainly are not a bodhisattva.
Why is this so? It is because the nature [of reality] is fundamentally empty and quiescent, perfectly formed as a whole. When one gives rise to this...
The mind is nothing more than self-awakening and self-cultivation; in reality, there is no dharma that gives rise to this *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* mind.
Subhūti, what do you think? Did the Tathāgata obtain any dharma from the Buddha Dīpaṃkara by which he attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*?

“Did the Tathāgata attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*? “No, indeed, World-Honored One. As I understand the meaning of what the Buddha has taught, there is no dharma by which the Buddha attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* at the place of the Buddha Dīpaṃkara.
The Buddha said, “So it is, so it is, Subhūti. Truly, there is no dharma by which a Tathāgata attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.”

Subhūti, if there were any dharma that the Tathāgata had attained as *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, then the Buddha Dīpaṃkara would not have bestowed upon me this prediction: "In a future age, you shall become a buddha named Śākyamuni.
Because, in reality, there is no dharma by which one attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, therefore...
Dīpaṃkara Buddha bestowed upon me this prediction, saying: "In a future age, you shall attain Buddhahood and be named Śākyamuni.
Why is this? "Tathāgata" means the suchness (*tathatā*) of all dharmas.
Subhūti, if anyone should say that the Tathāgata has attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, in truth there is no dharma by which the Buddha has attained it.

"Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. Subhūti, as for the Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi attained by the Tathāgata, therein there is neither reality nor unreality. Therefore, the Tathāgata says that all dharmas are Buddha-dharmas.
Subhūti, what is called 'all dharmas' is precisely not all dharmas; therefore it is so named."
"All dharmas. [Note:
This refers to the meaning taught by the Buddha, namely that which was stated above: "In reality, there is no dharma that gives rise to the bodhicitta.
"Thus it is, thus it is" means that these words profoundly accord with the Buddha's own mind. Śākyamuni; in the language of China, this means "The Able One" (Nénrén). This signifies that—
The nature of the mind is pure and complete; it encompasses all things. "Muni" (牟尼) is the Chinese term for "silence.
This means that the essence of the mind is fundamentally quiescent, such that movement and stillness do not cause it to shift. Silence is its substance (*tǐ*), which is *Tathatā* (Suchness);

benevolence is its function (*yòng*), which is *Āgata* (Coming). The reason "Śākya" is mentioned first and "Muni" follows is to show the subsuming of function back into the substance. In total, this is one single Reality.
The nature [of the Buddha] is designated as Śākyamuni when a title is added; he is generally referred to as the Tathāgata, or as the Buddha.
"All phenomena" refers to all mundane and supramundane phenomena. "The meaning of the suchness of all phenomena" means the meaning of the true suchness (*tathatā*) of all phenomena;
it is a direct penetration to the fundamental essence of the Tathāgata, wherein in reality there is no phenomenon whatsoever. Within this—
Within true nature (*tathatā*), the mind is fundamentally empty and still; it is utterly devoid of form and characteristics (*nimitta*). Therefore, there is no substantial form or characteristic.
The locus of emptiness is the actual locus of true nature; therefore, there is no unreality. In the preceding fascicle, "neither real nor unreal" was spoken in terms of phenomena (*dharma*);
here, it is spoken in terms of the mind. Since all phenomena are *bodhi*, it is said that "all dharmas are Buddha-dharmas. This cannot [be otherwise].
One does not seek awakening as something separate from all phenomena. However, since all phenomena are not real, people provisionally rely upon them for practice;
therefore, it is said that "phenomena are themselves non-phenomena. One must not, within these phenomena, cling to the existence of an awakening.

Treatise: This statement clarifies the meaning of the Tathāgata’s lack of attainment regarding any dharma while in the presence of Dīpaṃkara Buddha, thereby demonstrating that there is no dharma for the realization of the fruit.
Since there was originally no dharma from which he generated the aspiration for enlightenment, how could there be any dharma by which he attained the fruit?
In essence, the Tathāgata is the Buddha of True Nature (*dharmatā*). This true nature pervades the worlds of empty space and remains eternally as it is.

Furthermore, it manifests in accordance with the conditions of those who perceive it; illumination arises from stillness, and clarity emerges from emptiness, like a bright mirror suspended in the void.
When objects come before one, one responds to them as if they were real objects; yet, like a shadow passing by that leaves no trace, the fundamental essence remains intact.

Therefore, one is named "Tathāgata" (Thus-Come One). My true essence is inherently *tathatā* (suchness) from the very beginning. Its manifestation within all phenomena is likewise spontaneous and natural:
it comes forth as a responsive expression, yet departs without lingering. This is the meaning of "suchness" (*tathatā*), which is immovable. It is non-existent.
The "Dharma-cloud" is not a state of dull emptiness or nihilistic annihilation. True Suchness (*tathatā*) is profoundly tranquil; it does not establish a single dharma, yet all dharmas are suchness.
It does not abandon a single dharma, yet it is neither dharma nor non-dharma, being both dharma and non-dharma.
It is the totality of the single Bodhi-Dharmadhātu—this is what is meant by the principle that "all dharmas are suchness. To know only that True Suchness is the essence of all dharmas is...
Know that the Dharma is not obtained from without.
The Buddha taught that in unsurpassed bodhi, there is not only no dharma that can be produced, but also no dharma that can be attained.
"In the past, at the place of my original teacher, Dīpaṃkara Buddha, was there ever any dharma that could be obtained for unsurpassed bodhi?
Subhūti replied, "I understand the meaning of what the Buddha has said: at the place of his original teacher, the Buddha attained the Way of bodhi through self-nature and self-awakening;
there was no secret transmission. The Buddha certified these words.
He said: "It is so, it is so. In truth, there is no dharma by which one attains this bodhi.

If there were such a dharma, then when Dīpaṃkara Buddha earnestly and repeatedly raised up what he had attained himself and transmitted it to me, he would not have merely granted me a single prediction, saying:
'In a future age, you shall become a buddha named Śākyamuni. It is only because—"
That which is "non-attainment" is the wondrous fruit of realization; it is the dharma-gate inherently possessed within the stage of nature (*prakṛti-bhūmi*).
Thus, Dīpaṃkara Buddha merely conferred a prediction (*vyākaraṇa*); how could he have ever obtained any dharma from another? Why is this so? A Tathāgata does not depart from all dharmas;
rather, it is the meaning of being "self-so" (*svayambhū*) amidst all dharmas. Or, there may be someone who says, "I have attained this Bodhi..."
He said, "I do not know that I have truly come from the state of non-existence.
However, the reason I have attained this Dharma is entirely due to the Bodhi within my pure mind. This awakened nature is fundamentally without form or trace;
this Dharma has no substantial color or appearance. Emptiness itself is Bodhi; this Dharma is not false. It is precisely as it is said:"
Form is emptiness; emptiness is form. For this reason, the Buddha taught that all these dharmas are the Dharma of Prajñā.
However, because the human mind has not yet attained clarity, it must rely on this Dharma to point the way from delusion and eliminate the four marks.
Once true emptiness is realized, I have personally attained it; even the Dharma is not existent. Only then can it be called the Buddha-Dharma.

“Subhūti, it is as if, for example, there were a person with a large body. Subhūti said, “World-Honored One, when the Tathāgata speaks of a person with a large body, that is precisely not a large body;
it is merely designated as a ‘large body. Subhūti, it is the same for a bodhisattva.
If one should say, ‘I shall bring immeasurable sentient beings to parinirvāṇa,’ then that one is not called a bodhisattva. Why is this? Subhūti...
In reality, there is no dharma called a "bodhisattva. Therefore, the Buddha has said that all dharmas are without self, without person, without sentient being, and without life-span.
Subhūti, if a bodhisattva were to say, "I shall adorn the buddha-fields," he would not be named a bodhisattva.
Why is this? What the Tathāgata calls "adornment of the buddha-fields" is, in fact, not [adornment].
“Subhūti, this adornment is called ‘adornment. If a bodhisattva penetrates the dharma of non-self, the Tathāgata says that he is truly a bodhisattva.
*Annotation:* The first paragraph establishes a metaphor to introduce the subsequent text. The unreality of the "great body" serves as a simile for all dharmas.
The fundamental non-existence [of the body] is like the phrase "the human body is large and tall.

Before the Buddha had finished speaking these words, Subhūti did not wait for him to conclude his discourse but spoke directly. That which is not a "great body" is that which lacks the characteristics of a body;
that which is called a "great body" is the true nature of reality (*dharmatā*), vast and boundless. It is also like this. Following the preceding meaning, he speaks of bodhi...
The *sattva* has no characteristic of self, just as the Buddha has no characteristic of a body. If one speaks of these three phrases, one first uses the inverse statement to clarify them;
why? Because of the four phrases, one then correctly explains their meaning.
Within the sutras, the terms "Tathāgata" and "Bodhisattva" appear interchangeably and in various contexts; each of these has its own subject and object regarding the teaching of the Dharma.
In this regard, the Tathāgata is the host and the expounder is the guest, for all expounding is fundamentally based upon the Tathāgata’s entrustment.

When speaking of practice, the Bodhisattva is the host and the Tathāgata is the guest; for while this sutra specifically addresses the Bodhisattva’s generation of the resolve, it takes the Tathāgata as its standard and guide.
Regarding the phrase "no-self" (anātman), the character for "self" (ātman) serves as a contrast to what precedes it.
The two instances of the word "self" refer to penetrating the dharma of non-self, which is pure and fundamental, entirely without obstruction.
A true Bodhisattva who has reached a state of absolute purity and freedom from artifice is one at the stage of Equal Enlightenment (Samyaksambodhi).

Treatise: This proclaims that there is no one who saves sentient beings, yet there is the saving of them; that there is no adorning of the Buddha-land, yet there is its adornment. It demonstrates the Bodhisattva’s dharma of non-self.
Saving sentient beings is great compassion, and adorning the Buddha-land is great wisdom; both are matters within the Bodhisattva’s own domain.
However, if there is even a single thought of self, one is no longer a Bodhisattva. If one knows that dharmas are empty and without self, [one directly...]
Upon attaining great enlightenment, one realizes that all marks are empty; this is precisely the realm of true awakening.
For humans and sentient beings, the root of the "life-span self" (jīvātman) arises from the notion of a self. The Buddha therefore employs the Dharma of forgetting form and detaching from marks.
All are subsumed within non-self. Later in the text, it further states: "The dharma of non-self achieves the stage of patience (kṣānti).
This further demonstrates the method for people to descend and abide [in that state]; it is the most essential point within the sutra.
The Discourse: The Buddha asked Subhūti, "For example, suppose there were a human body that was both tall and large.
Subhūti replied, "When the Tathāgata speaks of a human body being tall and large, it is not a truly large body; only the Dharma-body is called a large body.
The Buddha said, "A Bodhisattva is without the mark of self, just as the Buddha is without the mark of a body."
Furthermore, if a bodhisattva were to say, "I have brought immeasurable sentient beings to parinirvāṇa," this would imply that there is a dharma by which beings are saved.
Could such a person still be called a bodhisattva? Why is this? Because true nature is empty, void, and utterly transparent;
in reality, there is no dharma that can be named "bodhisattva. It is precisely because a bodhisattva attains [this state] through purity that they are so named.
This is called "ear. Therefore, when the Buddha speaks of all dharmas, it is nothing other than to guide sentient beings so that they may awaken to their original nature.

Since the self, person, multitude, and life-span are fundamentally devoid of the four marks, how can one become attached to the mark of a single sentient being and say, "I shall deliver these beings"?
If a Bodhisattva makes such a statement as, "I shall adorn the Buddha-lands," this is attachment to marks.
Can such a person still be called a Bodhisattva? For what reason? That which the Tathāgata calls the adornment of Buddha-lands is, in fact, the adornment of the mind’s land.
The land of the mind is without marks and is fundamentally pure; how could it require adornment?

To remain unstained by the six sense objects and to maintain constant concentration and wisdom—this is what is called adornment. Now, to give rise to a mind of deliverance while becoming attached to adornment...
One who possesses these marks of severity cannot be called a bodhisattva. Ultimately, what kind of mind must one arouse to be truly named a bodhisattva?
It is one who penetrates everywhere with unobstructed understanding, profoundly clarifies the dharma of non-self, and remains far removed from all marks;
the Tathāgata calls such a person a true bodhisattva.
"Subhūti, what do you think? Does the Tathāgata possess a fleshly eye? "Not so, World-Honored One; the Tathāgata possesses a fleshly eye.
"Subhūti, what do you think? Does the Tathāgata possess a divine eye? "Not so, World-Honored One; the Tathāgata possesses a divine eye.
"Subhūti, what do you think? Does the Tathāgata possess a wisdom-eye? "Not so..."
"Venerable One, the Tathāgata possesses the eye of wisdom. Subhūti, what do you think? Does the Tathāgata possess the Dharma-eye?
"Not so, World-Honored One; the Tathāgata possesses the Dharma-eye. "Subhūti, what do you think? Does the Tathāgata possess the Buddha-eye?
"Not so, World-Honored One; the Tathāgata possesses the Buddha-eye. "Subhūti, what do you think? Regarding the Ganges River..."
"Regarding all the sands within the Ganges River, the Buddha says they are sands; it is not otherwise, World-Honored One, that the Tathāgata says they are sands.

Subhūti, what do you think? If there were as many Ganges Rivers as there are grains of sand in a single Ganges River, and if there were as many Buddha-worlds as there are grains of sand in all those Ganges Rivers—would these be many? "They would be very many, World-Honored One."
The World-Honored One told Subhūti: "In all those lands, the Tathāgata fully knows the various kinds of minds of all sentient beings.
Why is this? The Tathāgata says that all minds are 'non-minds'; it is only by way of designation that they are called 'minds.
And why? Subhūti, the past mind cannot be apprehended; the present mind cannot be apprehended; the future [mind]..."
The mind cannot be apprehended.

*Commentary:* To perceive forms and colors is the fleshly eye (*māṃsa-cakṣus*). To illuminate the great trichiliocosm universally is the divine eye (*divya-cakṣus*). For the candle of wisdom to be ever-luminous is the wisdom eye (*prajñā-cakṣus*).
To realize that all phenomena are empty is the dharma-eye (*dharma-cakṣus*). For the fundamental nature to be eternally awakened is the Buddha-eye (*buddha-cakṣus*). Wisdom...
The essence of wisdom universally illumines the entire dharma-realm; it is metaphorically likened to the eye, which is precisely what is meant by *prajñā*.

"Sands of the Ganges" means that each grain of sand represents one Ganges River. While the former "sands of the Ganges" were used as a metaphor for generosity (*dāna*), these "sands of the Ganges" serve as a metaphor for world-systems.
Wherever there is a world-system, there must necessarily be a Buddha to provide instruction and transformation.
This is called a Buddha-world. This metaphor has five levels: first, counting the sands by means of the Ganges River;
second, taking each grain of sand as a river and counting the rivers; third, calculating worlds based on all those grains of sand; fourth, calculating all sentient beings within those worlds;
and fifth, calculating the minds of those sentient beings, which arise and perish in myriad forms, just like these sands.
"Many" refers to the minds of sentient beings, which are minds of perversion. "Various kinds" refers to the sense that their meanings cannot be enumerated in detail.
This encompasses the three periods of past, present, and future. "Non-mind" refers to the mind of deluded conceptualization.
This is not the true fundamental mind. That which is called "mind" is the fundamental mind when no deluded thoughts arise.
To think of past events is the past mind; to think of present events is the present mind; to think of future events is the future mind.
Within a single thought-moment of an ordinary person, there are thus the past, the present, and the future.
"Come! You must see it as alive; you must not say it cannot exist. Commentary:
This reiterates the meaning that the Tathāgata knows all and sees all, demonstrating the essential method for subduing the mind.
"Eye" (cakṣus) takes the sense of observing and illuminating. The Tathāgata possesses these five eyes and contemplates the deluded minds of sentient beings.
The fetters: one harbors lingering attachment toward things of the past, clinging adherence toward things of the present, and anticipatory longing toward things of the future.
Sentient beings wander to and fro, driven solely by these three mental states, drifting through birth and death.
The Tathāgata, with the three characters "unattainable," pierced through the delusions of the masses; the firewood of desire, though piled high, was suddenly extinguished.
Entering the cool clarity: though delusions and karma have long entangled one, liberation is established. Once the mind has departed, one immediately attains the Bodhi-mind.
While phenomena come and go, the mind remains without stagnation. Empty throughout the three periods of time, it is profoundly still, vast, and pure.
It is like polishing a mirror: when the grime is exhausted, its brilliance appears. The fundamental essence of my own mind is thus. This is what the Tathāgata spoke of in the sutras.
At this point, the state of the Samādhi of the Mind Arising Without Abiding has been fully and clearly revealed.
The Master explains that the Buddha, wishing to elucidate the minds of sentient beings, first poses a question:
"The Tathāgata possesses the physical eye for observing emanation bodies, the celestial eye that universally illumines the great trichiliocosm, and the Prajñā that is eternally luminous."
The wisdom-eye; the Dharma-eye that realizes the emptiness of all phenomena; and the Buddha-eye of the eternally awakened self-nature.
"Do these five eyes exist? Subhūti replied to each of these questions, saying, "The Tathāgata possesses the five eyes. The Buddha then raised the world as a further question, asking:
"If one were to take the sands of countless Ganges Rivers and use them to count the worlds of the Buddhas, would they not be many indeed?"
"Is it so? Subhūti replied that it was indeed very many. The Buddha said:
"In as many lands as there are, all sentient beings therein each possess a mind; however many such kinds of minds there may be, the Tathāgata perceives and knows them all with his pure five eyes.
Why is this? Because all minds spoken of by the Tathāgata [are as he has described]."
All these are the deluded minds of sentient beings; they are not the true mind that eternally abides within the nature.
When one realizes that the deluded mind is no-mind, the fundamental essence of the Bodhisattva is seen. This is what is called "mind. Why is this so?

It is because the past has already perished, the present is fundamentally empty, and the future does not yet exist. Yet sentient beings cling to what has passed, calculate what exists [in the present], and conceptualize what is to come.
As they arise, these three minds appear in profusion; how could these three minds ever be made to abide?
If one can attain purity, there will be neither "three minds" nor "no three minds," and with not a single thought arising, the whole body [of reality] manifests spontaneously.
Thus, it can be known that sentient beings do not ultimately remain as sentient beings.
"Subhūti, what do you think? If someone were to fill a trichiliocosm with the seven treasures and give them as a gift, would that person, by reason of this, acquire much merit?
"It is so, World-Honored One; that person would acquire very great merit by reason of this.
"Subhūti, if merit had any substantial reality, the Tathāgata would not say that one 'obtains' it."
"Because there is no merit, the Tathāgata says that one obtains much merit.

*Annotation:* Regarding "causes and conditions": it is because of the merit of giving that one takes this as the condition for obtaining blessings. What was previously called "much merit" refers to the merit of recitation;
what is here called "much merit" refers to the cultivation and realization of the ultimate fruit. The meanings taken are distinct.
Separate.

Treatise: This is the sixth comparison of merit. While the preceding passages all compared [the treatise] with the excellence of the sūtra, this merely compares the presence or absence of the nature of merit, without mentioning the upholding or recitation; thus it differs from the nature of merit in the previous [sections].

These teachings correspond with one another from afar. As for worldly blessings—wealth, nobility, fame, and achievement—people perceive them as having substantial reality, yet they do not realize that when such merit is exhausted, they will fall and continue to undergo the cycle of rebirth (*saṃsāra*).
Therefore, I do not speak of the abundance of worldly merit. As for supramundane merit, it is pure and unconditioned;
it does not appear to be "merit" in the conventional sense, yet it is capable of delivering one from the ocean of birth and death and bringing about great liberation.
Because it is joyful, it is said that the merit is great. This is the stage of ultimate perfection; therefore, it does not mention "upholding" or "reciting.
The Buddha told Subhūti: "If there were someone who, with the seven treasures filling a trichiliocosm..."
"If one uses this for the sake of giving, will the fruit of its merit be great? Subhūti answered that it would be very much so.
The Buddha said, "If the merit of such giving results in the enjoyment of glory and splendor by the person, others may see it as having substantial reality;

yet, upon investigation, it does not transcend the conditions of karma and will eventually be exhausted. Therefore, the Tathāgata does not say that such merit is great. However, if [it arises] from within one's nature..."
Regarding merit: though one’s own mind is pure, people consider it non-existent. Yet, when investigated to its fundamental nature, the Tathāgata is never exhausted.
Therefore, the Tathāgata says that the merit obtained is vast.
General Explanation: From "Again Requesting to Dwell" down to this point, there are five sections comprising one unit. All of these clarify the meaning of the preceding volume.
First, the Buddha spoke of the non-substantiality of the resolve for enlightenment (*bodhicitta*); next, he spoke of the non-substantiality of the realization of the fruit;

and finally, he spoke of saving sentient beings and adorning the buddha-lands—all of which are devoid of self or dharmas. Furthermore, by means of the five eyes, he refutes the three minds; thus, both mind and dharmas are empty.
Right view and prajñā are the pure, unconditioned, and wondrous realm; within them, merit and virtue are spontaneously present, equal in measure to empty space.
How could they ever be spoken of as being on the same level as the causes and conditions of material giving?
"Subhūti, what do you think? Can the Buddha be seen by means of a body of perfect physical form? No, World-Honored One;
the Tathāgata should not be seen by means of a body of perfect physical form. Why is this?
What the Tathāgata calls a 'body of perfect physical form' is itself not a body of perfect physical form; it is merely designated as a 'body of perfect physical form. Subhūti, what do you think?"
“Can one perceive the Tathāgata by means of his possession of the various marks? No, World-Honored One.

The Tathāgata should not be perceived by means of his possession of the various marks. Why is this? The Tathāgata has said that the possession of the various marks is itself non-possession; it is merely called the ‘possession of the various marks.’”
Commentary: "Endowed" means without any deficiency. "Endowed with the form-body" refers to the eighty minor marks (anuvyañjana);
these are the manifestations of the Buddha-dharma in the body. "Endowed with all the marks" refers to the thirty-two major marks (lakṣaṇa);
these are the manifestations of the Buddha-dharma in the physical characteristics. "One can see the Tathāgata through the former" refers to those who wish to perceive [the Buddha] by means of form.
The Tathāgata Satkāyadṛṣṭi said: "This so-called 'Tathāgata' can be seen. This means that there is a physical form (*rūpalakṣaṇa*) of the Tathāgata that can be perceived by people.

"It should not" means that it is certainly not the case that he can be seen through marks (*lakṣaṇa*), yet it is also not the case that he cannot be seen through marks; therefore, it is said "it should not. This differs from "cannot."

Commentary: This passage reiterates that the Tathāgata cannot be perceived by means of physical characteristics (*rūpalakṣaṇa*), thereby demonstrating that ultimate emptiness (*śūnyatā*) is fundamentally devoid of form and appearance.
The previous statement that "he cannot be seen through characteristics" meant that physical characteristics are not the true characteristic; the characteristic itself is not the Buddha.

The present statement that "he cannot be seen through characteristics" means that the absence of characteristics (*alakṣaṇa*) is itself the characteristic; the absence of characteristics is not non-Buddha. Form...
The body originally manifests from within the pure *dharmakāya*; this is form that is formless.
The marks and signs (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*) originally flow forth from within the true reality of *tathatā*; these are signs that are signless.
Therefore, to grasp at form and signs as the *dharmakāya* is certainly not possible; yet, to seek the *dharmakāya* apart from form and signs is likewise not possible. Thus, the Tathāgata is...
Form is not non-form; one should not see the Tathāgata through form, for he is signless. Signlessness is not non-signlessness;
one should not see him through signs, for that would be incomplete. This "incompleteness" clarifies the True Body (dharmakāya), while this "completeness" clarifies the Responsive Body (nirmāṇakāya).
"Should not" and "is not"—these names are, in essence, of a single meaning.
The Buddha said, "Subhūti, can the Buddha be seen by means of a body of perfect form? Subhūti replied, "No, Tathāgata;
one should not see the Buddha by means of a body of perfect form. Why is this? Because a body of form is a physical frame of flesh and blood, not the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).
If it were the Dharma-body, it would be without change and without decay, and every thought-moment would be nothing other than *prajñāpāramitā*."
If so, how could the eighty minor marks possibly confine it? Within the physical body (rūpakāya), there exists a wondrous physical body;
this is called the "endowed physical body. The Buddha asked: "Can a Buddha be seen by means of his fully endowed marks? Subhūti replied: "No.
A Tathāgata should not be seen by means of his fully endowed marks. Why is this? Because..."

The various marks of perfection that have been described here are not to be grasped merely as external characteristics. Through the contemplative illumination of Prajñā, all phenomena are entirely integrated.
As for the six supernormal powers and the eight liberations, they are eternally fulfilled within one's own intrinsic nature.
Within this Tathāgata of Wondrous Marks, there is the Tathāgata of True Nature. This is called the perfection of all marks.
Subhūti, do not think that the Tathāgata has the thought, "I shall preach some Dharma.
Do not have such a thought. Why? If anyone says that the Tathāgata has preached some Dharma, they slander the Buddha; they cannot understand.
"Subhūti, that which I have taught as 'the teaching of the Dharma' is a dharma that cannot be taught; it is for this reason called 'the teaching of the Dharma.
*Annotation:* The upper "nian" (thought) character refers to the thought of the Tathāgata himself. The lower "nian" character refers to the thoughts of sentient beings.
Those who slander the Buddha are said to believe [his words] yet fail to understand them, thereby falling into the view of calumny. There is no dharma...

That which can be spoken refers to the fact that, from the very beginning, there are no phenomena. This is called "one who preaches the Dharma," meaning one who demonstrates to others the principle of the true reality of ultimate emptiness, enabling people to awaken to it for themselves.

Treatise: This explains the intention behind the Tathāgata’s teaching that there is no dharma he has preached, thereby demonstrating that in ultimate emptiness (*śūnyatā*), fundamentally no dharma exists.

The Buddha repeatedly instructed people not to cling to the conventional expressions of written words, but rather to use the wondrous principle of ultimate emptiness as a seal for the buddha-nature inherent within all sentient beings. Originally, he preached the Dharma with a mind that abides nowhere.

It is simply that those who desire to understand must penetrate the true nature. Regarding all phenomena (*dharma*), the actual nature of all phenomena is a wondrous essence of emptiness and stillness;
fundamentally, there is not a single phenomenon to which one can become attached. Regarding myself, the awakened mind is pure; whether speaking or remaining silent, all is as it is.
Since from the beginning there is no dharma, what could possibly be said? Therefore, I speak while there is nothing to speak, and I do not speak while speaking. This is called "speaking."
This is the Dharma. When the Tathāgata was approaching his parinirvāṇa, Mañjuśrī requested that the Buddha remain in the world to turn the wheel of the Dharma once more.
The Buddha said, "I have remained in the world for forty-nine years, yet I have never spoken a single word. This is precisely the meaning.
The Buddha said: "Subhūti, do you see the Tathāgata as teaching and explaining to sentient beings every day, and thereby conclude that the Tathāgata has any dharma to speak?

You must not entertain such a thought. Why is this? If anyone says that the Tathāgata has taught any dharma, it means they do not understand the true nature of the Tathāgata; they are slandering the Buddha. This is because..."
"You are unable to understand the meaning of the emptiness of dharmas that I have taught.

Subhūti, what is called 'teaching the Dharma' is nothing more than speaking out of necessity in order to cause sentient beings to eliminate external delusions. In reality, true nature remains as it is;
fundamentally, there is no dharma that can be taught. To simply cause others to awaken to true emptiness for themselves—this is what is called 'teaching the Dharma.'"
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One, will there be any sentient beings in future ages who,
upon hearing this Dharma being taught, will give rise to faith? The Buddha said, "Subhūti, they are not sentient beings, yet they are not non-sentient beings."
For what reason? Subhūti, as for "sentient beings," the Tathāgata has said that they are not sentient beings; they are merely called "sentient beings.
(This passage of the sūtra is absent in the Qin translation but present in the Wei translation.)
Note: "Wisdom-life" (prajñājīvita) means being endowed with wisdom that penetrates both life and its nature; this refers to the roots of goodness planted under immeasurable Buddhas.
Although Subhūti had long possessed the faculty of wisdom (*indriya*), because his realization of the principle was not yet profound, true wisdom did not arise.
Upon hearing the time when the Tathāgata declared there is no dharma to be preached, the roots of goodness planted in the past suddenly [manifested].
Because [the Dharma] is revealed, this auspicious name was established. The phrase "in future ages" refers to both the period of the Semblance Dharma and the Final Dharma.

The previous question regarding sentient beings generating faith referred to the present; this refers to sentient beings of the future. The former involves generating faith upon hearing the spoken words and phrases of the scriptures;
this involves generating faith upon hearing this Dharma being expounded. Each has its own degrees of depth and shallowness. Regarding "hearing the exposition":
Dharma. Continuing from the preceding "speaking of non-speaking," sentient beings and Buddhas equally possess the true nature; therefore, it is said that they are not [ordinary] sentient beings.
Yet, because they turn their backs on the truth and pursue delusion, losing their original source, it is said that they are not without being sentient beings.

When the Tathāgata says "they are not sentient beings," he is clarifying the phrase "they are not [ordinary] sentient beings. When he says "this is called sentient beings," he is clarifying "not without being sentient beings."
The Section on Birth. Treatise:
This statement declares that all sentient beings are, in their very nature, not sentient beings; it demonstrates that the characteristics of sentient beings are equivalent to emptiness.

The Buddha taught that while one arouses the mind, there is nothing to be aroused; while one attains the fruit, there is nothing to be attained; and while one delivers [beings], there is nothing to be delivered.
Born, yet there is nothing to be delivered; adorned, yet there is nothing to be adorned. One does not see [the Buddha] by means of physical marks, nor by the name of his preaching the Dharma.

Subhūti understood each of these points individually, yet he feared that future sentient beings, hearing of this "Dharma of non-dharma" and this "preaching of non-preaching," would be unable to believe and understand it, and thus would lack the means to settle their minds therein. For this reason...

Question: The Buddha taught that "Dharma" is the nature of True Suchness (*tathatā*). Sentient beings possess Buddha-nature; one life produces one Buddha, and many sentient beings produce many Buddhas.
Although they have not yet awakened the resolve for enlightenment (*bodhicitta*) nor realized the fruit of fruition, they cannot yet be hastily called anything other than sentient beings.
Yet, among the various modes of birth—womb, egg, moisture, and transformation—there are still those who undergo transformation and escape their ordinary, mundane state.
How much more so regarding human beings! One should naturally cause the view of sentient beings to vanish; they are not sentient beings, yet they are not non-sentient beings.
This is the point where the Tathāgata transforms sentient beings. To speak of "sentient beings" again is to sigh and awaken them;
it is as earnest and urgent as the phrase "these various sentient beings" in the aforementioned sutra.
Lecture: At that time, the Elder Subhūti, his mind opened and his understanding awakened, addressed the Buddha, saying:

"World-Honored One, after the age of the Dharma’s decline, will there be any sentient beings who, upon hearing this teaching of the non-dharma and this discourse on the unspeakable, will give rise to faith?
The Buddha said: "The Buddha and sentient beings equally possess this true nature of Prajñā. Although they are sentient beings..."
Yet the true nature is originally present; it cannot be designated as "sentient beings.
Although they are not sentient beings [in their ultimate state], because karmic conditions are manifest, they also cannot be designated as "non-sentient beings. Why is this?
For all these so-called sentient beings, if they can hear the Dharma of Prajñā and reverently believe in it, they will see their nature in an instant. This is precisely...
"What the Tathāgata has taught is not a 'sentient being'; it is merely a provisional designation for a 'sentient being.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying: 'World-Honored One, when the Buddha attained Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, was there anything obtained?
The Buddha said: 'So it is, so it is, Subhūti. Regarding Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, I [attained] nothing.'"
This unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment is such that not even the slightest dharma can be apprehended;
this is called *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Furthermore, Subhūti, this dharma is equal, without high or low; this is called *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi is attained by practicing all wholesome dharmas while being without self, without person, without sentient beings, and without life-span.
Subhūti, that which is called "wholesome dharma" by the Tathāgata is precisely not a wholesome dharma;
it is merely designated as a "wholesome dharma. (In some alternative editions, the character "ji" [precisely] does not appear before "fei shanfa" [not a wholesome dharma].)

Commentary: Previously, the Tathāgata spoke of "non-attainment," yet he has now spoken of "that which is attained. Śūnyatā (Emptiness) gives rise to this realization; thus, it accords with the realization of the Truth and brings forth what had not been brought forth.
For this reason, it is highly approved by the Buddha. The previous statement that "there is no attainment regarding dharmas" was made solely in reference to the essence of emptiness and quiescence.
This present statement—that "there is not even the slightest dharma to be attained"—is an analytical investigation that reaches the ultimate refinement and subtlety.
The subtle realm refers to the essence of bodhi-awakening; it is the dharma of no-dharma, which is the true dharma.
"Equality" means that all who possess cognition must share the same substance; there is no distinction between high and low, for it is not that the sages possess it while ordinary beings lack it.
Cultivating wholesome dharmas does not lie outside of Prajñā; the single character "wholesome" (śubha) is used as a marker to distinguish them from the māras and externalists.
Furthermore, the Buddha feared that sentient beings might develop attachment to wholesome dharmas; therefore, he refuted them by means of both wholesome and unwholesome dharmas.
Treatise: This further explains that no dharma can be grasped, and it demonstrates that even the characteristics of bodhi must be empty.

Furthermore, there is not even the slightest dharma; this is the unsurpassed mind. It is the equality of the essence of *tathatā* (suchness); it is the perfectly equal mind. It is the characteristic of *tathatā*.
To cultivate wholesome dharmas through non-self is the mind of perfect enlightenment; it is the function of *tathatā*. The Buddha’s answer is threefold:
first, he speaks in terms of the awakening-nature being empty and quiescent; second, he speaks in terms of the characteristic of equal awakening; third, he speaks in terms of cultivation.
The Dharma-awakening employs words; this is entirely for the purpose of guiding future generations. The Tathāgata does not retain a single dharma, yet he penetrates all dharmas.
Although there is not the slightest dharma, one must not enter into annihilation by means of "no-dharma.
Although it is equality, one must not rely upon equality as being eternally real. To cultivate all wholesome dharmas—this is pointing directly at [the truth].

Regarding the practical application of these teachings: one should take the absence of the four marks as the *nirvāṇa-hetu* (causal condition for realization) and the cultivation of the six perfections as the *pratyaya-hetu* (contributory condition).

Although it is said that "no dharma exists," it is also said that one should "cultivate wholesome dharmas with equanimity. Since it says to cultivate wholesome dharmas, it further states that they are "not wholesome dharmas.
At every step, one must look back toward the dharma of signlessness (*animitta*), never losing the essential principle that there is neither reality nor unreality.
He always desires that people awaken their nature through the Dharma, yet he also requires them to leave the Dharma behind to see the Truth. Commentary:
Having heard the meaning of there being no dharma that can be preached, Subhūti was suddenly enlightened and attained realization. He addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One, now that the Buddha has attained unsurpassed bodhi, is it not as if you have obtained something regarding the Dharma?
The Buddha deeply affirmed his words, saying: “So it is, so it is. Regarding the Dharma of unsurpassed, right, and perfect enlightenment, I did not obtain it from without;
rather, it is my own true nature. Within this true nature, all is vast emptiness and voidness; the spirit is concentrated and wisdom is extinguished.”
There is not even the slightest dharma that can be apprehended; this is called unsurpassed bodhi. The Buddha addressed Subhūti once more, saying:
"This dharma of unsurpassed bodhi is my own original nature. It does not increase in sages, nor does it decrease in ordinary beings.
Every person is fully endowed with it; it is equal, without high or low. For this reason, it is named unsurpassed bodhi."
Why is this? Because within my true nature, there has originally been no delusion of self, person, multitude, or life-span.

If one can uproot these entirely, and furthermore cultivate this wholesome dharma of clarifying the mind and seeing its nature, awakening oneself and awakening others, until emptiness and clarity are perfected, one will immediately attain unsurpassed Bodhi.
Subhūti, that which I call "wholesome dharma" is intended to provide a connection...
To lead sentient beings into the gateway of the Way, there was originally no such thing as these wholesome dharmas; it is merely by means of these provisional names that people are awakened.
One should know that what is called "wholesome dharmas" is the true nature. How could the true nature be described in terms of something attained?

Subhūti, if there were someone who took all the heaps of the seven treasures as numerous as all the Sumeru kings in a trichiliocosm and used them to practice giving, and if another person were to receive,
uphold, read, recite, and explain to others even as little as a four-line verse from this Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, the former merit would not equal even a hundredth part of the latter.
It does not approach even a hundred-thousand-million-billionth part, nor can it be reached by calculation or analogy (the Shijing edition lacks the character "recitation";
above "hundred-thousand-million-billionth part," there is no character "hundred").
Note: Previously, the Ganges River’s sands were used as a metaphor for their great number; here, Mount Sumeru is used as a metaphor for their magnitude.
This means that the quantity of the seven treasures gathered together is as vast and high as this mountain.

Commentary: This is the seventh comparison of merit. Because the preceding section spoke of cultivating wholesome dharmas, there may be a fear that people will suspect there are other wholesome dharmas to be cultivated apart from Prajñāpāramitā, and fail to realize that the six perfections ultimately converge in the departure from marks (*animitta*).
The visible, perfect Dharmakāya does not exist apart from the pure Dharmakāya;
that which is called "all Buddha-dharmas" emerges entirely from this sutra—this is no empty word.

Therefore, the name of the Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra is pointed out to show that from beginning to end there is nothing but a single principle, and that unsurpassed Bodhi does not transcend this Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra.
[This is merely] a name; apart from this, there are no other wholesome dharmas.
The Buddha told Subhūti: "In a trichiliocosm, all the Sumeru Kings of Mountains may be said to be vast and numerous.
Suppose one were to take a heap of the seven treasures equal in measure to these..."
The abundance of such mountains is used for giving; is the resulting merit not great? Yet, if one’s own nature is deluded, how can merit save them?

If a person receives and upholds this Prajñā Sūtra, even a single four-line verse, and gains its realization within their heart, or explains it so as to benefit the world, then they shall attain the fruit of Buddhahood above and deliver sentient beings below. Compared to this—
The merit of giving gifts of the seven treasures does not equal even one hundred thousand million billionth part of this sutra.
How can people not uphold this sutra?
*Huìjiě* (Comprehensive Explanation): From "From the Buddha’s ability to be fully endowed with a physical body" to this point, there are five sections that constitute one unit.
This also extends the meaning of the preceding fascicle. It is not "complete," for it sweeps away all previous notions of the physical body;
there is no "preaching the Dharma," for it sweeps away all previous notions of preaching the Dharma; it is not a "sentient being," for it sweeps away all previous notions of a sentient being;
there is not even the slightest dharma that is not a wholesome dharma, for it sweeps away all previous notions of *bodhi*. This is entirely the light of Prajñā-wisdom.
All phenomena are empty and devoid of marks; their nature and wisdom are both derived from this sutra.
For this reason, the name of the *Prajñāpāramitā* Sutra is pointed out here to compare its merit, thereby demonstrating that this sutra is worthy of being upheld and maintained.
Subhūti, what do you think? You should not think that the Tathāgata has this thought:
"I shall deliver sentient beings. Subhūti, do not have such a thought. Why is that? In reality, there are no sentient beings whom the Tathāgata delivers.
If there were sentient beings whom the Tathāgata delivered, then the Tathāgata would possess a self, a person, a sentient being, and a life-span. Subhūti...
The Tathāgata says that those who speak of a self do not have a self, yet ordinary people think they have a self.

Subhūti, those whom the Tathāgata calls "ordinary people" are, according to the Tathāgata, not ordinary people; they are merely designated as "ordinary people. (The phrase "they are merely designated as 'ordinary people'" is absent in all ancient editions.)

Note: "Sentient beings" refers to the nine types of sentient beings. "Ordinary persons" refers to human beings. The preceding [phrase] regarding "sweeping away and delivering beings" is spoken from the perspective of a bodhisattva;
this [phrase] is spoken from the perspective of a Tathāgata.
Commentary: This reiterates the statement that there is no one who saves sentient beings while clarifying that within the equal Dharma-realm, there are no marks of self or other.
The first half of the verse states that in saving sentient beings, one does not dwell upon the merit thereof;

the second half states that in reality, there is no dharma by which they are saved, and furthermore, that there is no self or dharma in the act of saving—this resides solely within the person of the Bodhisattva.

It is said that [these teachings] have never been spoken regarding the body of the Tathāgata. The Buddha feared that people might doubt whether the Tathāgata truly delivers sentient beings, or that they might perceive his various acts of protective mindfulness and entrustment as substantial dharmas, failing to realize that the Tathāgata is without self.

Since dharmas are fundamentally non-dharmas, and ordinary beings are fundamentally no ordinary beings, there is delivering yet no one delivered. This brings about the realization that, in truth, there is no case of nirvāṇa. By means of the Buddha...
This serves as an exemplar for bodhisattvas. For the Tathāgata is without self; who, then, delivers sentient beings?
An ordinary person is no different from a non-ordinary person; what sentient beings are there to deliver? Thus, awakening is equal, and the delivering of sentient beings is likewise equal.
Awakening is devoid of self and others; the delivering of sentient beings is likewise devoid of self and others.
The Buddha said to Subhūti: "Do not think that the Tathāgata has the thought, 'I shall have the intention to transform and deliver sentient beings.
Do not harbor such a thought. Why is this? Because of the true nature of Prajñā."
All beings are fully endowed [with this nature]. Although the Tathāgata delivers them by means of the Dharma, he delivers what they already possess;
he does not add to what they originally lacked. In truth, there is no sentient being who is delivered by the Tathāgata.

If one were to say that sentient beings are necessarily transformed and delivered by the Tathāgata, then the Tathāgata would possess the private notions of self, person, multitude, and life-span. The Tathāgata...
Since the four marks do not exist, why is it that at times when the Dharma is being taught, the word "I" is used?
You should know that when the Tathāgata speaks of a self, he does so in reference to ordinary people. That which is spoken of as having a self is not actually a self;
yet ordinary people think, "I alone am the one who can cross over. However, this nature of the Buddha is the same as the nature of ordinary people, Subhūti.
"Disciples, those who are called ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) by the Tathāgata are not, in fact, ordinary beings. For if an ordinary being can awaken to their own nature, they are the Tathāgata;
it is merely a conventional designation that they are called 'ordinary beings. This is what is meant by the equality of all dharmas."
"Subhūti, what do you think? Can the Tathāgata be perceived by means of the thirty-two marks?
Subhūti replied, "So it is, World-Honored One; so it is. The Tathāgata can be perceived by means of the thirty-two marks.
The Buddha said, "Subhūti, if the Tathāgata could be perceived by means of the thirty-two marks, then a Cakravartin Wheel-Turning King would also be a Tathāgata. Subhūti said:
The Buddha said, “World-Honored One, as I understand the meaning of what the Buddha has taught, one should not perceive the Tathāgata by means of the thirty-two marks.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses: “If one sees me by form, Or seeks me by sound, Such a person follows a deviant path And cannot see the Tathāgata.”
Note: "Contemplation" (guān) and "vision" (jiàn) are not the same. Vision perceives from without; contemplation carries the sense of looking up with reverence.
The Wheel-Turning Sage King (Cakravartin) refers to the Four Great Heavenly Kings, who, like the turning of a wheel, govern the four continents.
Those who observe the good and evil of human beings do so through the retribution of karma and the accumulation of merit; they likewise possess the thirty-two marks.

"Form" (rūpa) refers to the supreme and wondrous reward-body, which is the physical manifestation of the Tathāgata. "Sound" (śabda) refers to names, phrases, and sentences, which is the aspect of the Tathāgata’s preaching of the Dharma.
Although the term "self" (ātman) points to the Dharma-body, it is the self of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), which is unconditioned and markless.
It is the essence of pure wisdom. "Heresy" refers to non-Buddhist paths. The Tathāgata is the essence of true, eternal purity, one who is suchness (*tathatā*) and immovable.
"Unable to see the Tathāgata" means being unable to perceive the true nature of suchness.
This has the same meaning as the preceding passage: "To see that all marks are no-marks is to see the Tathāgata."

Commentary: This statement clarifies that one should not grasp at the characteristics of dharmas (*dharmalakṣaṇa*), and demonstrates that one must not become attached to signs when beholding the Tathāgata.
One cannot see the Tathāgata by means of signs. Subhūti has repeatedly answered this in great detail; why, then, does he now answer with "thus" (*evam*)?
It is because "observing" (*anupaśyanā*) and "seeing" (*darśana*) are not the same. "Seeing" refers to taking signs to be the Buddha.
Regarding contemplation through marks: although these are not the Buddha himself, the primary and secondary marks originally manifest from within the markless.
Thus, it is not improper to use these marks as a means to contemplate the subtlety of the markless; however, this was not the intention behind the Buddha’s question.
If those who have only recently resolved to attain enlightenment were to hear this, they might inadvertently enter onto a wrong path; therefore, the Buddha cut it off at the head.

Although the word "I" (Aham) points to the Dharmakāya, one can see that within the bodies of sentient beings there exists, each and every one, the essence of self-nature, which is pure, eternally true, and formless.
A student of the Buddha should seek this within their own mind; to seek the Buddha outside of this is [to stray].
This is a false path. To see is for sentient beings to see their own minds; it is not to see the Buddha of the Western Quarter.
These four lines of verse constitute a major pivotal point within this sutra.

The preceding four lines on the markless nature of the self find their resolution here, while the subsequent four lines on conditioned phenomena are illuminated by this. Thus, one cannot perceive [the Buddha] through marks.

Furthermore, the meanings such as "seeing the Tathāgata" and so forth are all collectively brought together and concluded within this verse. There are three ways to interpret the four lines of this verse:
the four lines on the mark of non-self (*anātman*) are verses on the dharma of the empty mind; the four lines on form (*rūpa*) are verses on the dharma of the empty body;
and the four lines on conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) are verses on the emptiness of worldly dharmas. [Attached for reference.]
The Buddha said to Subhūti: "Do you think that one can perceive the Tathāgata by means of the thirty-two marks?
Subhūti, not yet understanding his meaning, replied: "It is so, it is so.
One who wishes to perceive the Tathāgata does not do so apart from these thirty-two marks. The Buddha then enlightened him, saying: "Suppose..."
"If the Tathāgata could be perceived by means of the thirty-two marks, then a Wheel-Turning Sage King, who likewise possesses the adornment of a physical body, could also be called a Tathāgata.
Subhūti replied in accordance with the sound [of the teaching]:
"As I understand the meaning of the Buddha’s words, one should not perceive the Tathāgata by means of the thirty-two marks. At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:

It is said: The Dharmakāya is numinous awareness containing the truth; its wondrous substance is profoundly still and tranquil. It lies beyond the realm of physical traces and transcends the reach of ears and eyes.

If one merely seeks to behold my true nature by observing its countenance and form, or by listening to its voice and teachings, this is to be mired in the Buddha of the physical body (rūpakāya); such persons have all abandoned the correct path.
Those who follow false paths cannot see the Tathāgata.
Subhūti, if you should think that the Tathāgata attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi by means of marks that are fully complete, Subhūti, do not think thus;

it is not by means of marks that are fully complete that the Tathāgata attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. Subhūti, do not entertain such a thought. It is not by means of marks that are fully complete that the Tathāgata [attained it].

Therefore, Subhūti, you should not entertain the thought that one who has set their mind on *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* speaks of the annihilation of all phenomena; do not hold such a view. Why is this?
One who has set their mind on *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* does not speak of the annihilation of phenomena.
The Characteristic of Extinction (in an alternative version, the third phrase reads: "Because the Tathāgata is endowed with the marks of perfection," and lacks the character *wu*).
**Annotation:** "The extinction of all phenomena" means that all dharmas are completely annihilated and rendered useless.
"Not speaking of the characteristic of extinction regarding phenomena" means that practitioners must necessarily rely upon the Dharma of Prajñā as their cultivation.
These are the requisites for practice. If they were to be annihilated, they would be signless (*animitta*). Yet they are still called "signs" because of the attachment [to them].
This is divided into four sections. Regarding the first two sections, if one forms such a thought, do not form such a thought—both are presented together.
This speaks of the unacceptability of disparaging appearances. The following two sections clarify the reason for this, explaining why disparaging appearances is unacceptable.
Examining the Sixth Patriarch’s annotated edition, the third phrase of this chapter reads, "Because the Tathāgata possesses the marks of perfection," and contains no character for "not" (不).
Furthermore, in another version, "not" (不) is rendered as "it may be" (可以). According to these readings, the preceding [text]...
The first half-verse consists of one refutation and one formal exposition; its grammatical structure follows the same pattern as the second half.
Furthermore, it forms a complementary pair with the [passage on] "no cessation," making the meaning more clearly elucidated. This is noted here for reference.
Treatise: This statement clarifies that one should not grasp at the characteristics of non-dharmas, while demonstrating that the attainment of Bodhi cannot be characterized by cessation.
Throughout the Sūtra, both in its earlier and later sections, the central tenet is consistently the signless, the non-attainment, the unspeakable, and the non-existence of dharmas.

It is not the case that this [teaching] obstructs [reality] such that one would necessarily become attached to emptiness. One must understand that the Buddha merely teaches people to depart from signs; he does not...
Teaching people to destroy appearances is out of fear that they will become attached to appearances; it does not teach them to annihilate appearances.

Above, by means of detachment from appearances and non-self, the emptiness-aspect of *prajñā* was revealed so as not to fall into the view of eternalism. Here, by means of practicing the cause within appearances themselves, the true-aspect (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) of *prajñā* is revealed so as not to fall into the view of nihilism.
However, if one clings to formlessness, sinking into emptiness and abandoning existence, then all phenomena...
To sever and discard it would result in becoming like withered wood or dead ashes; therefore, the Buddha uses this [teaching] to refute that view.
By attaining this section, one comprehensively encompasses both emptiness and the provisional, concluding in the Middle Way—not merely through the two phrases "neither real nor unreal."
In this, the essential meaning is fully elucidated; furthermore, it is precisely the principle that [the Tathāgata] is not that which is named. In this, one purifies the spirit.
The Buddha addressed Subhūti, saying: "If you should think thus: 'The Tathāgata does not speak by means of the aggregate...'"

Regarding the marks of the feet: you should not entertain the thought that these sublime marks were attained by the Tathāgata through cultivation and perfection, and that they have no bearing on the fruit of Buddhahood, such that one could suddenly attain this unsurpassed bodhi.
Why must you not entertain such a thought? It is because those who give rise to the mind of Great Vehicle perfect enlightenment do not cling to existence, nor...

Do not fall into emptiness. If you should think thus: "One who has resolved for bodhicitta says that all dharmas must be annihilated, and therefore views the Tathāgata as empty and quiescent," do not entertain such a thought. Why is this?
One who has resolved for bodhicitta must necessarily rely upon the dharma of prajñā as the instrument for their practice. Regarding...
Regarding all dharmas, I do not speak of their annihilation. While it is certainly improper to cling to signs, can signs themselves be extinguished?

Subhūti, if a bodhisattva were to take the seven treasures filling worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges and offer them in charity, and if there were another person who, knowing that all dharmas are without self, attained the patient endurance (*kṣānti*) [of non-arising], this latter bodhisattva would surpass the former.
